title: Machines of Borrowed Grace
subtitle: Where a Language Model Gets Its Meaning, and Where Its Makers Get Theirs
author: Anonymous
lead: Whether a machine can think is a question about what it is for anything to mean something.
Language models now do work that used to take a mind. What are they, where do their words get their meaning, and what are the companies building them standing on?
description: This book asks what large language models actually are, where the meaning in their sentences comes from, and what the companies building them are relying on. It treats the machines as signs from end to end, numbers and tokens that mean something only because people trained them and people read them. It walks through ordinary examples like a word, a sum, a thermostat, and a sieve to show why the models can outperform most of us at coding, writing, and problem-solving without possessing a mind of their own. The first half stays close to the machine: how a sign comes to mean anything, whether a machine can think or feel, whether it can improve itself into understanding, and what would count as proof that it had. The second half turns to the people who make and sell the models, looking at the visions they offer of a future shaped by AI and the unstated assumptions those visions rest on.

The writing is plain and conversational, starting from everyday observations and building outward in the manner of Herbert McCabe explaining Aquinas. It draws mainly on Aristotle and Aquinas, with substantial help from Wittgenstein and more recent philosophers such as James Ross, while keeping technical claims about language models and their training tied to public sources. The author is explicit about working from a classical Christian frame, and the book moves from the philosophy of mind into questions of moral alignment, human dignity, and what a healed or flourishing human life would look like once AI is widespread.

Readers curious about AI beyond benchmark scores, especially those who wonder whether the technology requires any revision of older ideas about thought, meaning, or human nature, will find a sustained and accessible treatment here. It is less a technical survey of current models than a philosophical map of the territory the models occupy, written for anyone who wants to think through the claims that the machine understands, that alignment is the hard part, or that AI will deliver the good life, without needing prior training in either philosophy or machine learning.

title: Mere Catholicity
subtitle: What has been believed everywhere, always, and by all
author: Anonymous
lead: For the layman, it is all about 1054. The great wound in Christendom is not the changes of the last century. It is the Great Schism of 1054, when East and West tore apart, and so much of the later tearing follows from it.
description: For the layman, it is all about 1054. The great wound in Christendom is not the changes of the last century. It is the Great Schism of 1054, when East and West tore apart, and so much of the later tearing follows from it. The faith of the first thousand years is the ground the ancient churches still share. What each side defined after the tear it defined alone, and what a part defines alone cannot bind the whole until the whole comes to confess it. This book is a call to walk back, past every later rupture, to that first faith, and it is addressed to every house that still keeps a part of it, Roman, Orthodox, Anglican, Lutheran, Presbyterian.

For the theologian, the thesis is this. A council binds when the whole Body comes to confess the faith it defined, and binding by act alone never existed in the conciliar age, for the Body has been torn since 251 and reception across the open tears is attested wherever it has been checked. The church that refused Ephesus confesses, in Babai, the one Christ Ephesus defined. The churches that refused Chalcedon confess, in Severus, the faith it guarded. Measured by that record, the definitions added since the great schisms, Vatican I and the Marian dogmas on one side, the Palamite councils on the other, stand not yet received, never condemned, and the book denies both communions the same thing, the identification of the whole with a part. It keeps Newman's method while declining his authority, claims Ratzinger's Graz formula as lineage, quotes the ex sese clause rather than paraphrasing it and stands under its anathema, grades every disputed act of both millennia in an appendix, and lets its own rules cut against its own comfort, usury the hardest case, the veil left binding unless a retraction is shown. It closes with a proposal in Zoghby's genre made mutual, synodal professions by which each communion holds its post-schism definitions as patrimony rather than exacting them as conditions of communion.

And if this is true, then Tolkien and Lewis, the Roman Catholic and the Anglican who between them taught the last century's laymen to love the permanent things, are not divided now as they were at every altar on earth, and may well be smoking their pipes side by side in heaven, having a laugh with Luther, who swore he would sooner drink the blood of Christ with the papists than mere wine with the fanatics. And Dostoevsky is there too, the Orthodox among them, who always suspected heaven would be more crowded than the experts allowed. The hope of this confession is not more complicated than that.

title: Fifteen Sermons Preached before the University of Oxford
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Fifteen sermons from the University pulpit at Oxford, preached between 1826 and 1843, in which Newman asks how ordinary people come to believe and what reason has to do with their belief.
description: Newman preached these sermons in St Mary the Virgin, the University Church, before the assembled University. The first, The Philosophical Temper, First Enjoined by the Gospel, was given on Act Sunday in July 1826, and the last on the feast of the Purification in 1843. They were published together that year, and for a new edition in 1871 Newman added a dedication to his friend R. W. Church, then Dean of St Paul’s. The earlier sermons take up natural and revealed religion, the usurpations of reason, personal influence as the means of spreading truth, and the wilfulness of Saul. The sermons of 1839 to 1841 turn to faith itself, in Faith and Reason, contrasted as Habits of Mind, Love the Safeguard of Faith against Superstition, and Implicit and Explicit Reason. The volume closes with The Theory of Developments in Religious Doctrine.

Newman argued here that faith is a real exercise of reason, though not the kind of reasoning that waits on formal evidence. Most believers, he held, reason implicitly, from antecedent probabilities and a moral sense of what is likely to be true, and they often cannot state their grounds. He set this apart from explicit reasoning, which examines and defends those grounds afterward. He worked the argument out again in the Grammar of Assent of 1870. The last sermon, on Mary keeping and pondering the things she had seen, holds in small the case he made at length in the Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine. Philosophers of religion and historians of Victorian thought have read the volume closely, and it is a usual starting point for the study of his thought on belief.

This is No. 1 of Lérins Newman, the first title in its part The Anglican years, 1826–1845. Newman’s text is set from the NewmanReader transcription held in the site’s library, which follows the edition he prepared in 1871 with its dedication, advertisement and preface. The Editors of Mere Catholicity contribute a new introduction and explanatory notes on the people, books and controversies that Newman expected his Oxford hearers to know. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them. The book is issued as an annotated paperback and as a Kindle edition.

title: Two Essays on Biblical and on Ecclesiastical Miracles
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Two essays from either end of Newman’s years as a Fellow of Oriel, one on the miracles of Scripture and one on the miracles reported of the early Church, with his own later account of how the two fit together.
description: Newman wrote the first essay in 1825 and 1826 for the Encyclopaedia Metropolitana, as a sequel to a life of Apollonius of Tyana. It compares the miracles of Scripture with those reported elsewhere, in sections on the idea of a miracle, its antecedent credibility, its criterion and the direct evidence for the Christian miracles. He wrote the second in 1842 and 1843 as a preface to a translation of part of Fleury’s Ecclesiastical History. It asks how far the miracles of early Church history resemble those of the Bible, then weighs nine particular cases. Among them are the Thundering Legion under Marcus Aurelius, the cross seen in the sky by Constantine, the discovery of the Holy Cross, the death of Arius, and the fiery eruption that stopped Julian’s attempt to rebuild the Temple. In 1870 Newman issued the two together with a short advertisement.

The two essays give different answers to one question, and Newman said so. The first, which argues throughout with Hume, treats the miracles of Scripture as evidence addressed to inquirers and sets them well apart from later reports. The second, which answers among others Conyers Middleton’s Free Inquiry, treats the miracles of Church history as addressed to believers, as rewards of faith and matter for devotion, and finds their antecedent probability greater than the first essay allowed. In 1870 Newman wrote that the earlier essay had gone beyond the needs of its argument in disparaging later miracles, though he held that the two views were not inconsistent. Historians read the pair as a record of how his mind moved during the Oxford Movement. Philosophers read it for its treatment of probability and testimony.

Lérins Newman No. 2, in the part given to the Anglican years, 1826–1845, sets the essays from the NewmanReader transcription in the site’s library. That text follows Newman’s edition of 1870, with its advertisement and the bracketed remarks he then added at the foot of the page. A new introduction by the Editors of Mere Catholicity places each essay in its moment, and their explanatory notes identify the Fathers, historians and controversialists Newman cites. Newman’s own notes, early and late, stand as he left them. The edition appears in paperback and for Kindle.

title: The Arians of the Fourth Century
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s first book follows the Arian controversy from the schools of Antioch and Alexandria, through the Council of Nicaea, to the Council of Constantinople in 381, and asks why the Church came to fix its faith in creeds.
description: Newman wrote the book in 1831 and 1832 for Rivington’s Theological Library, at the invitation of Hugh James Rose. On its completion it seemed unfit for that series, and it appeared on its own in 1833, the year the Tracts for the Times began. The first chapter surveys the schools and parties in and about the ante-Nicene Church, among them the Church of Antioch, the Church of Alexandria, the Eclectic sect and the Sabellians. The second sets out the teaching of that Church on the Trinity and on the making of creeds. The later chapters narrate the Council of Nicaea and its consequences, the Eusebians, Semi-Arians, Athanasians and Anomoeans under Constantius, and the councils of Alexandria and Constantinople that followed. A chronological table and the original creed of Nicaea, as Socrates gives it, close the volume.

The book is a history written with a doctrine of the Church in view. Newman held that the Church of Alexandria guarded its mysteries by a discipline of reserve, teaching by stages, and that creeds were imposed only when heresy forced the Church to state what it had always held. He traced Arianism to the literal and critical temper of the school of Antioch rather than to Alexandrian Platonism. Later historians have largely set that thesis aside, and patristic scholarship has moved far from many of his sources and judgments. The book is still read as a guide to the mind of the Oxford Movement in its first year, with its regard for the Fathers, its sense of the ancient Church as a pattern for the English one, and Athanasius at the centre of its story.

As No. 3 of Lérins Newman, among the books of the Anglican years, 1826–1845, the history is set from the NewmanReader transcription in the site’s library. That text follows Newman’s third edition of 1871, with the enlarged tables, the appendix of longer notes and the bracketed references to his translation of Athanasius that he added then. The Editors of Mere Catholicity supply a new introduction and explanatory notes on persons, councils, terms and sources. Newman’s own notes are kept exactly as he left them. It is published in paperback and as a Kindle book.

title: Tracts for the Times
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The tracts Newman wrote for the series that gave the Tractarians their name, from his opening appeal to the clergy in 1833 to the later studies of the Breviary, the English divines and Purgatory.
description: The Tracts for the Times began in September 1833 with Newman’s Thoughts on the Ministerial Commission, Respectfully Addressed to the Clergy, and ran to ninety numbers by 1841. This volume gathers Newman’s own contributions as the site’s library holds them. The early tracts are short and pointed. They include The Catholic Church, Alterations in the Liturgy, The Episcopal Church Apostolical, The Gospel a Law of Liberty, the Heads of a Weekday Lecture and the letters on The Visible Church. Mortification of the Flesh a Scripture Duty, Primitive Episcopacy, Rites and Customs of the Church and The Grounds of our Faith follow. The longer tracts are the two Catena Patrum, which gather testimony from English divines to the apostolical succession and to baptismal regeneration, a study of the Roman Breviary with translated services, and On Purgatory. A course of daily prayers closes the book.

The tracts set out the claims on which the movement rested. Newman argued that the English clergy held their commission from the apostles by succession through the bishops, not from the State or the people, and that the Church of England was a branch of the Catholic Church bound to primitive doctrine and practice. The Catena Patrum were meant to show that these views had been taught by the English divines of the seventeenth century and were no novelty. The advertisement of 1834 states the aim as a practical revival of doctrines held by those divines but by then forgotten by most of the Church’s members. Supporters took the tracts as a recovery of the Church’s own inheritance. Critics in the 1830s took them as a step toward Rome, a charge Newman answered in the tracts themselves.

Lérins Newman No. 4, in the part covering the Anglican years, 1826–1845, sets these tracts from the NewmanReader transcription held in the site’s library, which reproduces them as J. G. F. and J. Rivington printed them in London, with their original advertisements. Tract 90 and the letters that followed it are in No. 19 of the collection. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the series and explanatory notes on the divines, Fathers, liturgies and disputes the tracts draw upon. Newman’s own notes are left as he wrote them. The volume appears in paperback and for Kindle.

title: Parochial and Plain Sermons, Volume 1
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The first of eight volumes of Newman’s parish sermons, opening with Holiness Necessary for Future Blessedness and Secret Faults, plain preaching on what it costs to take the Christian religion seriously.
description: Newman preached most of the Parochial and Plain Sermons to his congregation at St Mary the Virgin, Oxford, where he was vicar from 1828 to 1843. This first volume appeared in 1834, dedicated to Edward Bouverie Pusey. Its twenty-six sermons open with Holiness Necessary for Future Blessedness and The Immortality of the Soul, and go on through Secret Faults, Self-Denial the Test of Religious Earnestness and The Spiritual Mind. A group of four, Profession without Practice, Profession without Hypocrisy, Profession without Ostentation and Promising without Doing, examines the distance between what Christians say and what they do. Others treat times and forms of private prayer, the resurrection of the body and Christian reverence. The Religion of the Day, Scripture a Record of Human Sorrow and Christian Manhood come near the end.

The volume sets the tone for the series. Newman preached against what he called the religion of the day, a comfortable faith that kept the gentler parts of the Gospel and left the rest. He pressed instead on obedience, self-knowledge and the fear of God, and he held that holiness is the condition of being happy in heaven at all, since heaven would be no heaven to an unholy man. The manner is plain, with short sentences, close attention to motive and little ornament. Hearers at Oxford, many of them undergraduates, recalled the effect of his preaching for decades afterward. Readers in many traditions have since used these sermons as a guide to the moral life, often with little regard for the controversies of the period.

This book is No. 5 of Lérins Newman, the first of the eight sermon volumes in its part The Anglican years, 1826–1845. The text comes from the NewmanReader transcription in the site’s library, which follows the collected reissue of 1868 edited by W. J. Copeland, Newman’s former curate, whose preface is kept. The Editors of Mere Catholicity contribute a new introduction and explanatory notes on Scripture, the Prayer Book, and the people and opinions Newman addresses. Newman’s own notes stand as he left them. It is issued as an annotated paperback and as a Kindle edition.

title: Parochial and Plain Sermons, Volume 2
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The second volume of Newman’s parish sermons keeps the holy days of the Church year, from St Andrew in late November through Christmas, the feasts of the apostles and evangelists, and on to All Saints.
description: The second volume appeared in 1835, dedicated to Newman’s friend John William Bowden. Its thirty-two sermons follow the holy days of the Prayer Book calendar, beginning with The World’s Benefactors for St Andrew’s Day. Christmas brings The Incarnation, followed by Martyrdom for St Stephen, Love of Relations and Friends for St John the Evangelist and The Mind of Little Children for the Holy Innocents. The year runs on through St Paul’s Conversion Viewed in reference to His Office, The Reverence Due to the Virgin Mary, and sermons for Easter week and Whitsun week. Tolerance of Religious Error is for St Barnabas, Rebuking Sin for the Nativity of St John Baptist and The Danger of Accomplishments for St Luke. The volume ends on All Saints’ Day with Use of Saints’ Days.

The arrangement carries an argument. Newman wanted the English Church to keep the saints’ days its Prayer Book appointed, and he used each feast to draw a lesson from a life. The sermon on the Virgin Mary sets out the honour due to the mother of the Lord in terms an English churchman of the 1830s could accept, and readers have since compared it with what he wrote of her as a Catholic. The Incarnation states the doctrine of Christ’s person with the care of the Fathers he was then reading. Elsewhere the volume speaks of friendship, of the danger of riches and of accomplishments, of the Christian ministry, and of the Gospel as a trust committed to the Church. Its voice is the plain one of the first volume, turned toward the communion of saints.

Lérins Newman No. 6, in its first part, The Anglican years, 1826–1845, gives the volume from the NewmanReader transcription held in the site’s library, which follows the 1868 reissue of the Parochial and Plain Sermons under W. J. Copeland. The Editors of Mere Catholicity provide a new introduction and explanatory notes on the feasts, the texts and the writers Newman draws on. A reader can take the sermons in the order of the calendar, one for each holy day, or read the volume straight through. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them. The book appears in paperback and in a Kindle edition.

title: Parochial and Plain Sermons, Volume 3
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Old Testament lives from Abraham to Jeroboam, then the visible Church, baptism and the Daily Service, in the third volume of the parish sermons Newman preached at St Mary’s in Oxford.
description: The third volume appeared in 1836, dedicated to Robert Hurrell Froude, Archdeacon of Totnes, the father of Newman’s close friend Hurrell Froude, who died that year. It opens with five sermons on Old Testament figures, Abraham and Lot, Wilfulness of Israel in Rejecting Samuel, Saul, Early Years of David and Jeroboam. Then come Faith and Obedience, Christian Repentance, Contracted Views in Religion and A Particular Providence as Revealed in the Gospel, with Tears of Christ at the Grave of Lazarus and The Humiliation of the Eternal Son. The second half concerns the Church. Submission to Church Authority, The Church Visible and Invisible and The Visible Church an Encouragement to Faith lead to Regenerating Baptism and Infant Baptism. The Daily Service, Intercession and The Intermediate State close the book.

The sermons on Saul and David read character with close attention, finding in Saul a man of gifts undone by self-will and in David the patience of one who waited for God’s time. The later sermons bring the teaching of the Tracts into the pulpit. Newman held that the Church is a visible body with a ministry and sacraments, and that baptism gives the new birth it signifies. In The Daily Service he tells his own congregation why he had lately begun daily prayers in their church, as the early Christians had kept them. The Intermediate State describes the faithful departed as at rest in the presence of Christ, and argues against the doctrine of Purgatory as he then understood the Roman Church to teach it. The volume shows how closely his preaching and his controversy were joined.

No. 7 of Lérins Newman, in the part devoted to the Anglican years, 1826–1845, prints this volume from the NewmanReader transcription in the site’s library. That text follows the reissue of 1868 edited by W. J. Copeland. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction and explanatory notes on Scripture, the Prayer Book and the teaching Newman defends or answers. The sermons on baptism and the visible Church read well beside the Tracts for the Times, No. 4 in this collection. Newman’s own notes remain as he left them. The volume is published as an annotated paperback and a Kindle edition.

title: Parochial and Plain Sermons, Volume 4
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Sermons on the unseen world that surrounds ordinary life, among them The Invisible World, The Ventures of Faith and Watching, in the fourth volume of Newman’s parish preaching at Oxford.
description: The fourth volume is dedicated, in November 1838, to Hugh James Rose, Principal of King’s College, London, who in Newman’s words bade the clergy stir up the gift that was in them. Its twenty-three sermons begin with The Strictness of the Law of Christ and Obedience without Love, as instanced in the Character of Balaam, and go on to Moral Consequences of Single Sins and The Individuality of the Soul. A central group, The State of Grace, The Visible Church for the Sake of the Elect, The Communion of Saints and The Church a Home for the Lonely, treats the Church as the home of grace. Then come The Invisible World, The Greatness and Littleness of Human Life, Christ Hidden from the World, The Mysteriousness of our Present Being and The Ventures of Faith. Watching and Keeping Fast and Festival end the book.

Here Newman’s sense of the unseen is at its most direct. The Invisible World opens with the two worlds of the Creed, the visible and the invisible, and tells his hearers that “the world we do not see as really exists as the world we do see.” The Mysteriousness of our Present Being turns the same attention on the self, and Watching asks what it means to wait for Christ through ordinary days. The Ventures of Faith asks what a Christian has actually risked on the promises of God. The portrait of Balaam, a man who obeyed God without loving Him, has often been singled out by readers. Sermons from this volume appear in most selections of Newman’s preaching and are much quoted by writers on prayer.

Lérins Newman No. 8, in its first part, The Anglican years, 1826–1845, takes its text from the NewmanReader transcription in the site’s library, which follows W. J. Copeland’s reissue of the Parochial and Plain Sermons in 1868. A new introduction and explanatory notes by the Editors of Mere Catholicity accompany the sermons. Like the other volumes of the set, it can be read on its own, since each sermon was written to stand by itself before a congregation. The dedication to Rose is printed as Newman gave it, and Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them. The book appears in paperback and as a Kindle edition.

title: Parochial and Plain Sermons, Volume 5
author: John Henry Newman
lead: From Advent to the eve of Lent, the fifth volume of Newman’s parish sermons, with Unreal Words, The Thought of God, the Stay of the Soul, and a run of sermons on righteousness and on sin in the baptized.
description: The fifth volume appeared in 1840, dedicated to Joshua Watson, the layman whose long service to the Church Newman honours in the inscription. Its twenty-four sermons run in the order of the Church year from Advent to Quinquagesima. Advent brings Worship, a Preparation for Christ’s Coming, Reverence, a Belief in God’s Presence, Unreal Words and Shrinking from Christ’s Coming. Christmas brings Equanimity, The Mystery of Godliness and Christian Sympathy. The sermons for the Epiphany season include Righteousness not of us, but in us, The Law of the Spirit, The New Works of the Gospel and Transgressions and Infirmities. The Sundays before Lent close the book with Endurance, the Christian’s Portion, Affliction, a School of Comfort, The Thought of God, the Stay of the Soul, Love, the One Thing Needful, and The Power of the Will.

Two concerns run through the volume. The first is reality in religion. Unreal Words warns against professing more than one feels or means, and The Thought of God, the Stay of the Soul argues that the soul is made for God and can rest in nothing less. The second is the doctrine of justification, which Newman had treated at length in his lectures of 1838. Righteousness not of us, but in us and the sermons near it teach that the justified are made righteous by the presence of Christ within them, and are not merely accounted so. Transgressions and Infirmities distinguishes the infirmities that remain in the justified from the transgressions that forfeit their state. The sermons serve as a pastoral companion to the Lectures on the Doctrine of Justification, No. 15 in this collection.

This is No. 9 of Lérins Newman, in its part The Anglican years, 1826–1845. The sermons are set from the NewmanReader transcription held in the site’s library, following the eight-volume reissue of 1868 under W. J. Copeland. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction and explanatory notes, including notes on the seasons and Sundays the sermons were written for. The order of the Sundays is kept, so the book can be read through the winter season for which it was made. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them. It is published in paperback and for Kindle.

title: Parochial and Plain Sermons, Volume 6
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The sixth volume of Newman’s parish sermons follows the Church from the first Sunday in Lent through the Passion and Easter to Ascensiontide, Whitsuntide and Trinity Sunday.
description: The sixth volume appeared in 1842, the last of the six volumes of Parochial Sermons, and holds twenty-five sermons for the second half of the Church year. Lent opens with Fasting a Source of Trial, Life the Season of Repentance and Apostolic Abstinence a Pattern for Christians. The last two Sundays in Lent bring Christ, the Son of God made Man, The Incarnate Son, a Sufferer and Sacrifice and The Cross of Christ the Measure of the World. The Easter sermons include The Spiritual Presence of Christ in the Church, The Eucharistic Presence and Faith the Title for Justification. For Ascensiontide there are Rising with Christ and Waiting for Christ, and for Whitsuntide The Gospel Palaces, The Visible Temple and Offerings for the Sanctuary. Trinity Sunday closes the book with Faith without Demonstration, The Mystery of the Holy Trinity and Peace in Believing.

The volume holds Newman’s fullest Anglican preaching on the presence of Christ. The Spiritual Presence of Christ in the Church teaches that the ascended Lord is present to His people through the Spirit. The Eucharistic Presence, preached on the sixth chapter of St John, sets out a real presence of Christ in the sacrament while declining the doctrine of Transubstantiation, which Newman says the English Church does not admit. The Lent sermons treat fasting as a discipline the Church enjoins and describe the trials it brings. The Whitsuntide sermons on the Gospel Palaces and the Visible Temple defend the beauty of churches and the offering of wealth to them. Together these sermons give the sacramental teaching of the Oxford Movement as it was preached to a parish.

Lérins Newman No. 10, in the part given to the Anglican years, 1826–1845, sets the sermons from the NewmanReader transcription in the site’s library. That text follows the reissue of the Parochial and Plain Sermons edited by W. J. Copeland in 1868. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the seasons, the Scripture and the doctrine of each sermon. The order of the Church year is kept from Lent to Trinity Sunday. Newman’s own notes stand as he left them. The volume appears as an annotated paperback and a Kindle edition.

title: Parochial and Plain Sermons, Volume 7
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Eighteen sermons Newman gave to the Tractarians’ series of Plain Sermons, from The Lapse of Time at the turn of the year to The Crucifixion, Mental Prayer and Steadfastness in Old Paths.
description: Volumes 7 and 8 of the Parochial and Plain Sermons were first published in 1843 as the fifth volume of Plain Sermons, by Contributors to the Tracts for the Times, which was Newman’s own contribution to that series. The seventh holds eighteen sermons. It opens with The Lapse of Time, preached at the beginning of a new year, and continues with Religion a Weariness to the Natural Man, The World our Enemy, The Praise of Men and Temporal Advantages. The Season of Epiphany follows, with The Duty of Self-denial and The Yoke of Christ. Moses the Type of Christ and The Crucifixion lead into two sermons on the sacrament, Attendance on Holy Communion and The Gospel Feast. The book ends with Mental Prayer, Infant Baptism, The Unity of the Church and Steadfastness in Old Paths.

The sermons here are shorter than most in the series. Their theme is the natural reluctance of the heart toward religion and the discipline that slowly overcomes it, so that Religion a Weariness to the Natural Man is answered later by Love of Religion, a New Nature and Religion Pleasant to the Religious. Mental Prayer distinguishes prayer at set times and in set forms from the habitual prayer of a mind that keeps God in view. Attendance on Holy Communion presses the duty on those who stay away. The last sermon opens, “Reverence for the old paths is a chief Christian duty,” and asks its hearers to keep what the Church has received rather than seek discoveries in religion. Copeland later recorded that Newman had always doubted whether the word Plain suited the series.

No. 11 of Lérins Newman, in its part The Anglican years, 1826–1845, gives these sermons from the NewmanReader transcription held in the site’s library, which follows the eight-volume reissue of 1868 under W. J. Copeland. A new introduction by the Editors of Mere Catholicity explains how the volume came into the series, and their explanatory notes treat its Scripture, its references and its occasions. It pairs with No. 12, which holds the other half of the same original volume. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them. The book is issued in paperback and for Kindle.

title: Parochial and Plain Sermons, Volume 8
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The last volume of Newman’s parish sermons, with Divine Calls, The Call of David, Jeremiah, a Lesson for the Disappointed and The Shepherd of Our Souls, on how God calls and leads an ordinary life.
description: The eighth volume completes the set and, like the seventh, comes from Newman’s contribution of 1843 to the Plain Sermons, by Contributors to the Tracts for the Times. Its eighteen sermons open with Reverence in Worship and Divine Calls. A run of Old Testament lives follows in The Trial of Saul, The Call of David, Josiah, a Pattern for the Ignorant and Jeremiah, a Lesson for the Disappointed. Among them stand Curiosity a Temptation to Sin, Miracles no Remedy for Unbelief and Inward Witness to the Truth of the Gospel. The later sermons include Doing Glory to God in Pursuits of the World, Vanity of Human Glory, Truth Hidden when not Sought After, Obedience to God the Way to Faith in Christ and Sudden Conversions. The Shepherd of Our Souls, Religious Joy and Ignorance of Evil close the volume.

Divine Calls takes the call of Samuel as its text and holds that “we are not called once only, but many times,” so that the call is answered in prompt obedience to the duty at hand. The sermons on David and Jeremiah take up the same theme from Scripture, the one a youth called from the sheepfold, the other a prophet who saw little fruit of his labour. Sudden Conversions takes the case of St Paul and asks which kinds of apparently sudden change are what they seem. Doing Glory to God in Pursuits of the World asks how a Christian in trade or a profession may serve God in that work. Obedience to God the Way to Faith in Christ returns to the conviction that runs through all eight volumes, that obedience is the road by which faith grows.

This is No. 12 of Lérins Newman, the last of the eight sermon volumes in its part The Anglican years, 1826–1845. Its text is the NewmanReader transcription in the site’s library, following the reissue of 1868 edited by W. J. Copeland. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the Scripture and allusions of the sermons. Together with No. 11 it restores the single volume of 1843 that Newman gave to the Plain Sermons. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them. The volume appears in paperback and as a Kindle edition.

title: Essays from the British Critic
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Reviews and notices Newman wrote for the British Critic between 1836 and 1842, the quarterly he edited from 1838, on subjects from Archbishop Laud and Nicholas Wiseman to Exeter Hall and the Catena Aurea.
description: Newman began reviewing for the British Critic in 1836 and was its editor from 1838 until 1841, when he handed it to Thomas Mozley. This volume gathers articles of his from those years. They review Charles Webb Le Bas’s Life of Archbishop Laud, Edward Burton’s History of the Christian Church, Nicholas Wiseman’s Lectures on the Principal Doctrines and Practices of the Catholic Church, a life of the Pietist A. H. Francke, and the novel Geraldine, a Tale of Conscience. Later pieces take up Random Recollections of Exeter Hall, C. B. Elliott’s Travels in the Three Great Empires of Austria, Russia, and Turkey, Isaac Taylor’s Ancient Christianity with memoirs of Nicholas Ferrar, Godfrey Goodman’s Court of King James the First, the Protestant exiles of the Zillerthal, and the Oxford translation of the Catena Aurea of St Thomas Aquinas. A series of Notices of Books follows.

The reviews show Newman as a working critic and controversialist in the years of his widest influence at Oxford. The review of Wiseman’s lectures opens by saying the reviewer is no friend to Popery, yet welcomes a controversy that will teach English churchmen on what principles their Church stands. The article on Exeter Hall begins from the claim that religion is a social principle and goes on to the public meetings of the Protestant party held there. The review of the Catena Aurea sets the popular English picture of Aquinas beside a commentary he compiled from the Fathers. The shorter notices show the range of books an editor of the day had to handle. A few pieces carry the transcription’s note that Newman’s authorship is partial or uncertain. Historians of the movement read the whole for its temper between 1836 and 1842.

Lérins Newman No. 13, in the part covering the Anglican years, 1826–1845, sets these essays from the NewmanReader transcription held in the site’s library, which gives them as they appeared in the British Critic with the volume and date of each issue. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the review and its editor, and explanatory notes on the books, authors and quarrels under discussion. The articles run in the order in which they first appeared. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them. The book is published as an annotated paperback and a Kindle edition.

title: The Via Media, Volume 1
subtitle: The Prophetical Office of the Church
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s lectures of 1837 on the teaching authority of the Church, his fullest case for an English way between Rome and popular Protestantism, reissued forty years later with a long preface answering it as a Catholic.
description: The lectures grew, Newman says in the advertisement, out of parochial lectures delivered on weekdays, together with parts of a correspondence he had carried on with a member of the Gallican Church. They were published in 1837 as Lectures on the Prophetical Office of the Church, dedicated to Martin Joseph Routh, President of Magdalen College. After an introduction, the fourteen lectures treat the nature and ground of Roman and Protestant errors, the Roman teaching as neglectful of antiquity, the doctrine of infallibility considered morally and politically, and the use and abuse of private judgment. Later lectures take up the indefectibility of the Church Catholic, the essentials of the Gospel, Scripture as the record of faith and as the document of proof in the early Church, and the fortunes of the Church. In 1877 Newman reissued the book as the first volume of The Via Media.

This is Newman’s most sustained statement of the position the Tractarians called the via media. He argued that the Church of England held the faith of antiquity, tested by the rule of Vincent of Lérins, what has been taught “always, everywhere, and by all,” and that Rome had added to that faith while popular Protestantism had let much of it go. He distinguished an episcopal tradition, fixed in the creeds, from a wider prophetical tradition diffused through the life of the Church. In the preface of 1877 Newman, by then a Catholic, answered his own arguments. He set out the Church’s three offices, prophetical, priestly and regal, and explained the strains between them. Readers in both communions have studied the two texts together, the lectures and the reply written forty years later by the same hand.

As No. 14 of Lérins Newman, among the books of the Anglican years, 1826–1845, the lectures are set from the NewmanReader transcription in the site’s library. It follows Newman’s third edition of 1877, with the dedication, the prefatory notice, the advertisement of the first editions and the preface to the third. The Editors of Mere Catholicity supply a new introduction and explanatory notes on the divines, Fathers and controversies Newman engages. Newman’s own notes, Anglican and Catholic, are kept as he left them. It appears in paperback and as a Kindle book.

title: Lectures on the Doctrine of Justification
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s lectures of 1838 on how a sinner is made righteous before God, weighing the Lutheran account against the Roman and finding their meeting point in the indwelling presence of Christ through the Spirit.
description: Newman delivered these lectures at Oxford and published them in 1838, dedicated to Richard Bagot, Bishop of Oxford. The advertisement explains the occasion. Many serious readers believed that baptismal regeneration and the apostolical ministry fostered notions of human merit and conflicted with justifying faith, and Newman set out to show from Scripture that they did not. Lecture 1 considers faith as the instrument of justification, the view he associated with Luther, and Lecture 2 love as its formal cause, the view he took to be Rome’s. The middle lectures examine the senses of the word justification and the gift of righteousness, reaching Lecture 9, Righteousness the Fruit of our Lord’s Resurrection. The last lectures treat the office and nature of justifying faith, faith in relation to rites and works, and the preaching of the Gospel. An appendix discusses the formal cause of justification.

Newman’s thesis was that justification is both a declaring and a making righteous, and that the two meet in the gift of the Spirit, by whom Christ Himself dwells in the justified. On this account faith is the instrument on the side of the receiver and the sacraments the instrument on God’s side, and the righteousness given is neither a bare imputation nor a quality the soul holds apart from Christ. He meant the book as a statement of English divinity that might draw together parties who thought themselves opposed. Some historians of doctrine have disputed his reading of Luther. Others have found in the lectures a serious early attempt to bring Reformation and Tridentine teaching into conversation, and the book is cited in modern ecumenical discussion. Reissuing it in 1874, Newman wrote that he still held in substance what he had published in 1838.

Lérins Newman No. 15, in its part The Anglican years, 1826–1845, prints the lectures from the NewmanReader transcription held in the site’s library. That text follows the third edition of 1874, with the advertisements to the first and third editions. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the Reformers, the Fathers, Trent and the English divines whom Newman cites. The note on good works as the remedy of post-baptismal sin and the appendix on the formal cause are kept in their places. Newman’s own notes stand as he left them. The edition is published in paperback and for Kindle.

title: Lives of the English Saints
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Three Lives of hermits from the series of English saints Newman projected at Littlemore, St Gundleus of Wales, St Edelwald of Farne and St Bettelin of Stafford, told with open care about what can be known.
description: Newman projected the Lives of the English Saints at Littlemore in 1843 as a series of biographies of the saints of Britain, written by himself and his friends and issued in parts in 1843 and 1844. This volume holds three Lives of hermits from it. A Legend of St Gundleus tells of a Welsh king or chieftain of about AD 500, father of St Cadoc, who gave up his rule to his son and lived as a hermit. The History of St Edelwald concerns the hermit who followed St Cuthbert in his cell on Farne about AD 700, drawing on Bede. A Legend of St Bettelin tells of a hermit honoured as patron of Stafford toward AD 800, who sinned, repented and did penance. The volume ends with a miracle recorded at his church in 1386.

The three Lives are short, and they are as much a reflection on legend as a record of lives. In the opening of the Gundleus, Newman argues that where history is silent the Christian may meditate, filling in what Scripture or tradition has drawn in a few lines, as holy men had done before, without claiming to know more than is known. The Bettelin opens with the image of double stars that look like one in the sky, to explain why the stories of saints run together. Throughout he sets out what the sources say and what they do not. The series as a whole drew criticism in the 1840s for its handling of legend and miracle. These pieces belong to the last stage of Newman’s Anglican years, at Littlemore.

No. 16 of Lérins Newman, in the part devoted to the Anglican years, 1826–1845, sets the three Lives from the NewmanReader transcription in the site’s library. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the series and its reception, and explanatory notes on the places, chronicles and early British and English history behind each Life. The Lives are printed in the order Gundleus, Edelwald, Bettelin, with the titles and dates Newman gave each saint. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them. The volume appears as an annotated paperback and a Kindle edition.

title: Sermons Bearing on Subjects of the Day
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The sermons Newman published two months after resigning St Mary’s in 1843, on the Church, the world and the Christian’s duty in a time of trial, ending with The Parting of Friends.
description: Newman gathered these twenty-six sermons in 1843 and dated the advertisement November 25 of that year. All were preached in his parish of St Mary the Virgin, which took in the church at Littlemore, and in printing he added some passages of personal opinion that he had not thought fit for a parish congregation. The early sermons include The Work of the Christian, Saintliness not Forfeited by the Penitent and The Three Offices of Christ. A long sequence on the Church follows, from The Christian Church a Continuation of the Jewish to The Christian Church an Imperial Power and Sanctity the Token of the Christian Empire. Later come Wisdom and Innocence, Outward and Inward Notes of the Church, Grounds for Steadfastness in our Religious Profession and Elijah the Prophet of the Latter Days. The Parting of Friends closes the book.

The title is Newman’s own warning that these sermons bear on the circumstances of their day. The later ones were preached as he weighed the claims of the English Church after the censure of Tract 90 and the bishops’ charges against it. Outward and Inward Notes of the Church and Grounds for Steadfastness ask what marks a true Church and what holds a member to it. The Parting of Friends, preached at Littlemore in September 1843, takes leave of his people with the text of his first sermon of 1824, “Man goeth forth unto his work and to his labour until the evening.” In 1864 Charles Kingsley pointed to Wisdom and Innocence when he charged Newman with teaching that truth for its own sake need not be a virtue. Newman’s reply grew into the Apologia pro Vita Sua.

This is No. 17 of Lérins Newman, in its part The Anglican years, 1826–1845. It sets the sermons from the NewmanReader transcription held in the site’s library, which follows the reissue of 1869 edited by W. J. Copeland, to whom the volume is dedicated, with his preface and Newman’s advertisement of 1843. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the events and persons behind the sermons. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them. It is issued in paperback and as a Kindle edition.

title: An Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s account of how Christian doctrine grows across the centuries without ceasing to be itself, with seven notes offered to tell a true development from a corruption, written at Littlemore in 1845.
description: Newman wrote the Essay at Littlemore in 1845 and dated its advertisement there on October 6. A postscript records that while the book was in the press he joined the Catholic Church, and that the authorities to whom he offered it for revision preferred it to appear as he had written it. In 1878 he issued a revised and rearranged text, with a dedication to Samuel William Wayte, President of Trinity College, Oxford, which had made him once more a member of the college. The Introduction and first chapter treat the development of ideas in general. Chapters 2 to 4 give the antecedent and historical arguments, with instances from the doctrine of the Incarnation, the honour paid to Mary and the saints, and the papal supremacy. Chapter 5 sets out seven notes of a genuine development, and chapters 6 to 12 apply them to the history of the Church.

The Essay begins from a difficulty Newman says he had felt himself, that the teaching of the Church in later ages seems to differ from that of the first. His answer is that a living idea unfolds its aspects over time, in the minds of many, and that change of this kind can be the way an idea keeps its identity. Of such an idea he writes that “here below to live is to change, and to be perfect is to have changed often.” The seven notes, from preservation of type to chronic vigour, are offered as tests between growth and corruption. The book has shaped discussion of doctrine across the churches since it appeared. Roman Catholic theologians have taken up its account of development, while Anglican, Orthodox and Protestant readers have often contested its application to the papacy and to the doctrine of Mary.

No. 18 of Lérins Newman, the last but one in its part The Anglican years, 1826–1845, prints the Essay in the text of the edition of 1878, from the NewmanReader transcription held in the site’s library. It keeps the dedication and preface of 1878 and the advertisement and postscript of 1845. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the Fathers, councils, heresies and historians Newman cites. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them. The book appears in paperback and as a Kindle edition.

title: The Via Media, Volume 2
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s occasional writings of 1830 to 1841, from a letter on the Church Missionary Society to Tract 90 and its censure, gathered late in his life with notes he added as a Catholic.
description: This volume collects the shorter pieces in which Newman argued for the via media. It opens with Suggestions on behalf of the Church Missionary Society of 1830, and Via Media Nos. I and II, Tracts 38 and 41 of 1834, a dialogue between a clergyman and a layman. Then come a paper of 1835 on the restoration of suffragan bishops, Tract 71 On the Mode of Conducting the Controversy with Rome, a letter of 1837 on behalf of Pusey’s tracts on baptism, and a letter of 1838 to the Margaret Professor on Hurrell Froude’s statements concerning the Holy Eucharist. The centre of the book is Tract 90 of 1841, Remarks on Certain Passages in the Thirty-Nine Articles, with the letter of four college tutors, the resolution of the Heads of Houses of March 15, 1841, and Newman’s letters to Dr Jelf and to the Bishop of Oxford.

Tract 90 is the best known of the Tracts for the Times. Newman argued that the Thirty-Nine Articles, framed before the decrees of Trent were settled and aimed at the popular errors and abuses of their day, could be subscribed by one who held the Catholic faith of the early Church, and that they did not condemn Catholic doctrine as such. Four college tutors protested, the Heads of Houses censured the tract within weeks, and bishops charged against it. At his bishop’s wish the series came to an end. In the Apologia Newman traced his loss of confidence in his position to the months that followed. When he reissued these papers as a Catholic he added prefaces and bracketed notes, and the book ends with his retractation of the statements against the Church of Rome that he had made as an Anglican.

Lérins Newman No. 19 closes its part The Anglican years, 1826–1845. The text is the NewmanReader transcription held in the site’s library, which follows Newman’s collected edition and carries notes he dated as late as July 1883. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction and explanatory notes on the persons, offices, documents and university proceedings the papers assume. The papers are printed in the order Newman gave them, with the year of first publication at the head of each. Newman’s own notes, of both periods, are kept as he left them. The book is published as an annotated paperback and a Kindle edition.

title: Loss and Gain
subtitle: The Story of a Convert
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s first book as a Catholic is a novel of Oxford in the 1840s, in which an undergraduate listens, argues and reads his way out of the Church of England and into the Church of Rome.
description: Loss and Gain, subtitled The Story of a Convert, was published in 1848. Newman wrote it in Rome in the summer of 1847, while resident at Santa Croce, after a hostile tale about the Oxford converts had been sent to him from England. He judged that the fitting answer was a second tale. Charles Reding, a clergyman’s son at the invented St. Saviour’s College, spends the first two parts among tutors, friends and breakfast parties, hearing every opinion of the day on the Articles, the Fathers and the Church. Bateman, Carlton, Sheffield and Willis each stand for a different answer. In Part 3 Charles leaves Oxford, is besieged in his London lodgings by callers with a religion to recommend, and is received at a Passionist house in the east of the city, where Willis meets him again as Father Aloysius.

Newman’s Advertisement says the tale is not a work of controversy but a description of “the course of thought and state of mind” that ends in conviction, and that its principal characters are imaginary. That is how it reads. Much of the argument is given to people who disagree with Charles, often with sympathy and often with comedy, and the decisive moves happen in conversation and private reflection rather than in set debate. Early readers looked for real persons behind the characters, which Newman disclaimed in the same Advertisement. It is the lightest of his books in manner. It is also a close picture of the talk, manners and parties of Oxford in the Tractarian years, and historians of the university and of the Oxford Movement read it for that as well as for Newman’s account of conversion.

This is No. 20 of Lérins Newman and the first volume of its second part, the Catholic years 1848–1885. Newman’s text is set from the Newman Reader transcription of the uniform edition in its 1906 impression, which carries the original Advertisement of 1848, the Advertisement to the Sixth Edition of 1874 and the dedication to Charles W. Russell of Maynooth. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the writing of the novel and its place in Newman’s first Catholic years. Their explanatory notes identify the books, controversies, church practices and Oxford customs that the characters argue over, so that a reader without the period at hand can follow the talk. Newman’s own notes stand as he left them.

title: Discourses to Mixed Congregations
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Eighteen sermons from Newman’s first year as a Catholic priest in England, preached in a former Birmingham distillery to a congregation of Catholics and their curious Protestant neighbours.
description: Discourses to Mixed Congregations, published in 1849, was the first volume of sermons Newman issued as a Catholic. The Oratory of St. Philip Neri, which he had brought to England, opened its first Birmingham chapel in Alcester Street on 2 February 1849, and the opening discourse, “The Salvation of the Hearer the Motive of the Preacher,” was preached that day. There are eighteen in all. They run from the call to conversion in “Neglect of Divine Calls and Warnings” and “Faith and Private Judgment” to the doctrine of grace in “Nature and Grace” and “Illuminating Grace,” and close with “Mental Sufferings of Our Lord in His Passion” and two discourses on the glories of Mary. Newman dedicated the book to Nicholas Wiseman, then Vicar Apostolic of the London District.

The congregations were mixed in the sense that Catholics and Protestants sat together, and the discourses speak to both. At St. Mary’s, Oxford, Newman had read his sermons in a quiet and searching manner. These were written for strangers in a manufacturing town, at a time of strong feeling against Catholics, and they use direct appeal and a fuller rhetoric than anything he had published before. Readers have compared the two manners ever since, some preferring the Oxford pulpit and some the Birmingham one. The volume shows how Newman first set out the Catholic claims before an English audience after 1845. “Faith and Private Judgment” and “Faith and Doubt” put his case for authority in its plainest form, and the two Marian discourses state the devotion he defended again in the Letter to Pusey.

No. 21 of Lérins Newman, in the collection’s second part on the Catholic years 1848–1885, sets the text from the Newman Reader transcription of the uniform edition in its 1906 impression. Wiseman’s dedication and Newman’s notes to the discourses on grace, on the Catholic missioner and on the Passion are kept as he left them. To these the Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the founding of the Birmingham Oratory and the religious temper of the town in 1849, and explanatory notes on the Scripture, the Fathers, the saints and the Catholic practices to which Newman refers in passing, many of them unfamiliar to his first hearers as well as to readers now.

title: Sermon Notes
author: John Henry Newman
lead: For thirty years Newman went to his room after preaching and wrote down in brief what he had just said. These are those notes, the working record of his Sunday preaching as an Oratorian.
description: Sermon Notes was published in 1913 by the Fathers of the Birmingham Oratory from the small books in which Newman kept outlines of his sermons. Their introduction explains that after his conversion he gave up reading his sermons from a written text, and that most of these notes were written not before the sermon but after it. The first is dated 1 July 1849, on purity and love, and the last 9 June 1878, on the coming of the Holy Ghost at Pentecost. Between them come notes for the Sundays and feasts of the Church year, for the month of Mary and for the Brothers of the Oratory, on subjects such as purgatory, private judgment, the particular judgment, the name of Jesus, the Good Shepherd and the Immaculate Conception.

The notes are short, often a page or less, set out in numbered heads and half sentences, with the texts of Scripture marked and the course of the argument sketched. They show how Newman built a sermon, which points he chose for an ordinary Sunday congregation and how he came back to the same themes across the years. They also cover a long stretch of his life, from the first years of the Oratory through the 1860s and 1870s, for which few of his sermons were ever printed in full. Read beside his letters, they are a source for what occupied him week by week. They are also a practical model of plain preaching, of the kind he gave to a parish congregation and to the boys of the Oratory School rather than to a university pulpit.

No. 22 of Lérins Newman, in the part given to the Catholic years 1848–1885, takes its text from the Newman Reader transcription of the 1913 edition by the Fathers of the Birmingham Oratory, with their introduction and their dates and headings. The notes themselves keep Newman’s wording, abbreviations and numbered heads as he left them, and his own notes are kept in place. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on Newman as a Catholic preacher and on the history of the notebooks. Their explanatory notes expand his shorthand references, identify the Scripture and the feasts he names, and connect particular sermons to events in the Oratory and in Newman’s life.

title: Certain Difficulties Felt by Anglicans in Catholic Teaching, Volume 1
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Five years after leaving the Church of England, Newman spoke to the friends of the Oxford Movement who had stayed in it, and argued that the movement had never drawn its life from the national church.
description: Certain Difficulties Felt by Anglicans in Catholic Teaching, Volume 1 holds twelve lectures Newman gave in London in 1850, in the months after the Privy Council’s judgment in the Gorham case. The judgment had found for a clergyman whom his bishop had refused to institute over his views on baptismal regeneration, and many in the Oxford party asked whether their church could still be said to teach the faith. Newman addressed them directly. The first seven lectures take up the Movement of 1833, arguing that it was foreign to the national church and that its course led neither to a party within it, nor to a branch church, nor to a sect. The last five meet objections drawn from Catholic countries, from differences among Catholics, from separated bodies and from church history. The volume is dedicated to William Bernard Ullathorne.

The lectures are among Newman’s most pointed writing and among his most personal, since the men he spoke to had been his friends and followers. He argues from inside the Oxford Movement, turning its own principles on its members. His preface says he is not offering a direct proof of Catholicism but removing difficulties from the path of those who already admit the arguments for it. The tone is sharper than that of his Oxford writings, and Anglican readers then and since have said so. Historians of the Movement read the book for Newman’s own account of what 1833 had been about, written while the Gorham crisis was sending a second group of converts to Rome, among them Henry Edward Manning in the following year.

No. 23 of Lérins Newman belongs to the second part of the collection, the Catholic years 1848–1885. The text follows the Newman Reader transcription of the uniform edition in its 1901 impression, with the dedication, the preface of July 1850 and Newman’s notes kept as he left them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity supply a new introduction on the Gorham judgment and the state of the Oxford party in 1850, and explanatory notes on the persons, tracts, bishops and controversies Newman assumes his hearers know. The second volume of Certain Difficulties, which holds the letters to Pusey and to the Duke of Norfolk, appears in this collection as two separate books, Nos. 30 and 34.

title: The Present Position of Catholics in England
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s answer to the No Popery agitation of 1851 is a set of comic and angry lectures on how the English came to believe what they believed about Catholics, and why the story was so hard to correct.
description: The Present Position of Catholics in England holds nine lectures Newman delivered in Birmingham in the summer of 1851 to the Brothers of the Oratory, the laymen attached to his community. They came months after Pius IX restored the Catholic hierarchy in England in 1850, when meetings, sermons and the press were full of protest against “Papal Aggression.” Newman takes the Protestant view of the Catholic Church as his subject and examines, lecture by lecture, what he holds sustains it, from tradition and fable to prejudice, assumed principles and ignorance. The first lecture opens with the fable of the Man and the Lion. Shown a palace full of statues of men overcoming lions, the lion praises the art but remarks, “Lions would have fared better, had lions been the artists.” The last lecture turns to the duties of Catholics themselves.

Newman is at his most satirical here. He imagines, for instance, a Russian speaker who explains the British constitution to a Moscow audience from scraps of Blackstone, so that English hearers can feel what it is to be judged by a hostile tradition. The book had a cost. A passage in Lecture 5 on Giacinto Achilli, a former Dominican then lecturing against Rome, led to a prosecution for criminal libel in 1852, in which Newman was convicted and fined. The final lecture is often quoted for its call for an educated laity, “men who know their religion, who enter into it.” Historians of Victorian religion read the lectures as a record of anti-Catholic feeling at its height, and as one of the first sustained Catholic replies to it in English.

No. 24 of Lérins Newman, in the collection’s second part on the Catholic years 1848–1885, sets Newman’s text from the Newman Reader transcription of the uniform edition in its 1908 impression, with the dedication to Paul Cullen, then Archbishop of Armagh, the preface and Newman’s notes as he left them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the restoration of the hierarchy, the agitation that followed it and the Achilli trial. Their explanatory notes identify the newspapers, pamphlets, lecturers and popular books Newman quotes or parodies, many of which were household names in 1851 and are now forgotten.

title: The Idea of a University
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The discourses Newman wrote for the Catholic University in Dublin make the case that a university exists to teach knowledge as a whole, theology included, and to form a trained and cultivated mind.
description: The Idea of a University gathers two books under one title. The first is the nine discourses on university education that Newman wrote in 1852, after Paul Cullen and the Irish bishops had invited him to found a Catholic University in Dublin. The first five were delivered as lectures in Dublin in May and June of that year. The second is a set of ten lectures and essays from his years as rector, among them “Christianity and Letters,” “Literature,” “Elementary Studies,” “University Preaching,” “Christianity and Scientific Investigation” and “Discipline of Mind.” Newman brought the two together under the present title in 1873. The discourses run from “Theology a Branch of Knowledge” to “Knowledge its Own End” and “Knowledge Viewed in relation to Religion,” and the volume carries dedications to the university’s friends and benefactors and to William Monsell.

The argument is that knowledge forms one whole, that a university which leaves out theology leaves a gap that other sciences will fill badly, and that liberal knowledge is worth having for its own sake, as a habit of mind rather than a store of facts. Discourse 8 holds Newman’s portrait of the gentleman as “one who never inflicts pain,” which he presents as the fruit of liberal education and also as something distinct from Christian virtue. The discourses were written for a Catholic institution, but they have been read far beyond it, in arguments over the liberal arts, professional training, the research university and the place of religion in higher education. Secular and religious readers often quote the same chapters for different ends.

No. 25 of Lérins Newman stands in its second part, the Catholic years 1848–1885. Its text is the Newman Reader transcription of the 1907 impression of the uniform edition, with both parts complete and with Newman’s preface, dedications, advertisement and notes as he left them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity contribute a new introduction on the Dublin university, its founding and its difficulties, and on how the two halves of the book came together. Their explanatory notes cover the writers, institutions and educational schemes Newman names, from Bacon and Locke to the colleges and examinations of his own day, and give the context of the debates he enters.

title: Cathedra Sempiterna
author: John Henry Newman
lead: A short passage of Newman’s prose on the see of Peter and its endurance through persecution, invasion and revolution, drawn from his first Dublin discourse of 1852 and later printed on its own.
description: Cathedra Sempiterna, “the everlasting chair,” is a piece of about a thousand words. The Newman Reader notes that it was put together from passages in Discourse I of Newman’s Discourses on the Scope and Nature of University Education (1852), and reprinted in My Campaign in Ireland, the collection of his Irish university papers printed for private circulation in 1896. It opens with the voice of Peter as “a real authority,” then surveys the history of the papacy, the gathering of the Roman world into the Church, the coming of the northern peoples, the quarrels with kings and, in the generation before Newman, the struggles with Joseph of Germany and with Napoleon. It ends with a passage from Isaiah. A note added after the text records Newman’s barefoot visit to the shrine of St. Peter in Rome in January 1856.

The passage is oratory, written for an Irish audience at the start of a university the Holy See had urged on the bishops. Newman sets the authority of Peter at the head of the new undertaking and argues from history that the popes have met the crisis of every age. It states plainly a view of the papacy that he held throughout his Catholic life, and which he later set out with more qualification, in the Letter to the Duke of Norfolk of 1875 and elsewhere. The piece is read both as devotional prose and as evidence of how Newman spoke about papal authority twenty years before the Vatican Council. Readers of different traditions take it in different ways, but they agree on what it says.

No. 26 of Lérins Newman, in its second part, the Catholic years 1848–1885, sets the text from the Newman Reader transcription of the reprint in My Campaign in Ireland, with the transcriber’s note on its source and the closing note on the Roman visit. Because the piece is short, the Editors of Mere Catholicity give it a fuller frame. Their new introduction places it in the Dublin discourses of 1852 and in Newman’s writing on the papacy from the Apologia to the Letter to the Duke of Norfolk. Their explanatory notes explain the historical allusions, from the barbarian invasions to the Napoleonic wars, and the Scripture behind its close. Newman’s own text is printed as he left it.

title: Callista
subtitle: A Tale of the Third Century
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s second novel is set in Roman Africa in the year of the Decian persecution, and follows a Greek image-maker from the worship of the old gods to baptism and martyrdom.
description: Callista, subtitled A Tale of the Third Century, was published in 1855. Newman wrote much of three early chapters and sketched the character of Juba in the spring of 1848, then put the book aside until the summer of 1855, when he finished it quickly. The scene is Sicca Veneria, a hill town of Roman Africa, around the year 250, when the emperor Decius ordered sacrifice to the gods. Agellius is a lonely young Christian, his brother Juba a scoffer, their uncle Jucundus a dealer in images of the gods, and Gurta a witch. Callista, a Greek girl who models images for the shrines, is drawn to the faith through Agellius, through the priest Cæcilius, who is Cyprian of Carthage in hiding, and through the Gospel of St. Luke he gives her. A plague of locusts and a rising against the Christians bring the story to its end.

Newman’s Advertisement calls the book a simple fiction and an attempt to imagine, from a Catholic point of view, the feelings and relations of Christians and heathens in the third century. Its interest lies there more than in its plot. The pagan town is drawn with humour and some sympathy, Jucundus above all, a comfortable man who wants the gods kept for the sake of trade and order. Callista’s reasoning in prison, from the voice of conscience to the Person it answers to, follows a line Newman developed in his philosophical writing, and readers have often compared it with the Grammar of Assent. The book was undertaken, the Advertisement says, at a suggestion “from a high ecclesiastical quarter,” and it belongs with Wiseman’s Fabiola among the Victorian novels of the early Church.

No. 27 of Lérins Newman, in the second part, the Catholic years 1848–1885, gives the text of the uniform edition in its 1901 impression, from the Newman Reader transcription, with the dedication to Henry William Wilberforce, the Advertisement of 1855 and the postscripts Newman added to later editions. The Editors of Mere Catholicity provide a new introduction on the writing of the novel and its sources in Cyprian and in the history of the African Church. Their explanatory notes cover the places, cults, customs, Latin phrases and points of church history in the story. Newman’s own notes stand as he left them.

title: Sermons Preached on Various Occasions
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Fifteen sermons for great days, among them The Second Spring, preached before the bishops of the restored English hierarchy in 1852 on the return of Catholic life to England.
description: Sermons Preached on Various Occasions first appeared in 1857 and grew in later editions to fifteen sermons. The first eight were preached in the University Church in Dublin in 1856 and 1857, beginning with “Intellect, the Instrument of Religious Training.” The rest mark events in English Catholic life. “Christ upon the Waters” was preached at St. Chad’s, Birmingham, on 27 October 1850, at the installation of Ullathorne as the first bishop of the see, and “The Second Spring” at St. Mary’s, Oscott, on 13 July 1852, in the first Provincial Synod of Westminster. There are two sermons on the mission of St. Philip Neri for the Oratory’s first anniversary, sermons at the funerals of Bishop Weedall in 1859 and of James Hope Scott in 1873, and “The Pope and the Revolution” of 1866.

“The Second Spring” is the best known sermon Newman preached as a Catholic. It sets the restoration of the hierarchy in 1850 against three centuries of decline, in a sustained image of spring after a long winter, and it warns that the new life will meet suffering. It has often been reprinted as a piece of English prose. The Dublin sermons speak to the students and teachers of a new university on the relation of intellect and religion. The Oratory sermons describe St. Philip and the kind of community he founded, which Newman had brought to England. Together the sermons show him preaching on public occasions to the bishops, clergy and laity of a small church newly conscious of its place in English life.

No. 28 of Lérins Newman, in the collection’s second part on the Catholic years 1848–1885, follows the Newman Reader transcription of the uniform edition in its 1908 impression. That text includes the sermons added to the third and fourth editions, the dedication to Henry Edward Manning and the Advertisement of 1857. Newman’s notes, and his headnotes on where and when each sermon was preached, stay as he left them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the occasions themselves and on Newman’s public preaching in Dublin and Birmingham, and explanatory notes on the people named from the pulpit and on the Scripture and liturgy from which the sermons draw.

title: On Consulting the Faithful in Matters of Doctrine
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s essay of 1859 argues from the history of the Arian crisis that the belief of the laity is a witness to apostolic tradition, and that the Church has reason to take account of it.
description: On Consulting the Faithful in Matters of Doctrine appeared in The Rambler in July 1859, in the last number Newman edited. In May the magazine had said that the faithful are consulted in preparing a dogmatic definition, as they had been before the definition of the Immaculate Conception in 1854, and some readers objected to the wording. Newman, writing as an anonymous contributor, takes two questions in turn, what “consult” can mean and whether the faithful are in fact taken into account. He draws on the Roman theologian Perrone, whom he had met in Rome. The longest section turns to the fourth century and gathers extracts from the Fathers and historians, region by region, from Alexandria and Egypt to Antioch, Edessa, Cappadocia and Nicomedia, on the laity’s resistance to Arianism.

The essay’s central claim is that for much of the fourth century the Nicene faith was kept, in Newman’s words, “not by the unswerving firmness of the Holy See, Councils, or Bishops,” but by the consensus of the faithful, and that there was “a temporary suspense of the functions” of the teaching Church. The article was delated to Rome by an English bishop, and Newman stood under suspicion there for some years. It drew little notice outside Catholic circles until the twentieth century, when theologians took it up in discussions of the sense of the faithful and the place of the laity in the Church. It is now one of his most cited works, read by some as a charter for the voice of the laity and by others as a narrower historical argument about tradition.

No. 29 of Lérins Newman is part of the second division of the collection, the Catholic years 1848–1885. The text is set from the Newman Reader transcription of the article as it appeared in The Rambler for July 1859, with its two notes as Newman left them and its historical extracts complete. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on The Rambler, its editors and the dispute the article caused, and on the essay’s later reception. Their explanatory notes identify the Fathers, historians and theologians Newman quotes, explain his Latin, and set the Arian episodes he cites in their order.

title: A Letter to the Rev. E. B. Pusey on his Recent Eirenicon
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s reply to his old friend Pusey sets out what Catholics believe about the Virgin Mary, drawing on the Fathers, and separates that belief from the devotions that had grown up around it.
description: A Letter to the Rev. E. B. Pusey on his Recent Eirenicon answers the book in which Edward Bouverie Pusey, Newman’s colleague in the Oxford Movement, proposed grounds on which the Church of England and the Church of Rome might be reconciled, and named Roman devotion to Mary as a chief obstacle. Newman wrote his reply as a public letter to a friend. After introductory remarks and comments on statements in the Eirenicon, he sets out the belief of Catholics concerning the Blessed Virgin as distinct from their devotion to her, then that belief as coloured by devotion, and then Anglican misconceptions and Catholic excesses. Five notes follow, on the Fathers’ testimony that Mary is the Second Eve, on Suarez and the Immaculate Conception, on difficult passages in Basil, Chrysostom and Cyril, on the Greek Church and on a scandalous tenet.

The letter rests on a distinction Newman made central, between faith and devotion. The faith he finds in the second century, in Justin Martyr, Irenæus and Tertullian, who call Mary the Second Eve, and he argues that the later teaching on her holiness and her intercession grows from that early doctrine. Devotion, he says, varies with place and temper, and he disowns a number of extravagant statements Pusey had quoted from Catholic writers. The letter is one of the clearest examples of Newman applying his theory of doctrinal development to a single doctrine. It has remained a standard text in discussion of Mary between Anglicans, Catholics and Orthodox, and it records a friendship that survived twenty years of separation.

No. 30 of Lérins Newman, in its part on the Catholic years 1848–1885, takes its text from the Newman Reader transcription of the second volume of Certain Difficulties Felt by Anglicans in Catholic Teaching, in which Newman reprinted the letter, in the uniform edition’s impression of 1900. His five appended notes and his footnotes stand as he left them.
