The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on Pusey, the Eirenicon and the long friendship between the two men, and explanatory notes on the patristic, medieval and later authors Newman cites, from Justin Martyr to Suarez, and on the devotional books whose language Pusey had challenged.

title: Apologia Pro Vita Sua
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Charged in a magazine with holding that truth need not be a virtue, Newman answered with the history of his own mind, from his Evangelical boyhood to his reception into the Catholic Church in 1845.
description: Apologia Pro Vita Sua grew out of a quarrel. In January 1864 Charles Kingsley wrote in Macmillan’s Magazine that “Truth, for its own sake, had never been a virtue with the Roman clergy,” and named Newman. After an exchange of letters Newman decided that the only answer was a full account of his religious opinions, and he wrote it that spring in a matter of weeks, issuing it in weekly parts. In 1865 he reissued it without nearly a hundred pages of controversy, as a narrative in five chapters. Four give the history of his opinions to 1833, from 1833 to 1839, from 1839 to 1841 and from 1841 to 1845, and the fifth the position of his mind since 1845. Notes follow on liberalism, ecclesiastical miracles, the Anglican Church, the economy, and lying and equivocation.

The book is a defence of Newman’s honesty, and its method is to let the reader watch his mind move. He describes his first conversion at fifteen, his debts to Whately, Keble, Hurrell Froude and the Fathers, the Tracts for the Times and the Via Media, the force upon him in 1839 of the words “Securus judicat orbis terrarum,” Tract 90 and the years at Littlemore. The last chapter sets out what he holds as a Catholic on authority and infallibility. The Apologia changed English opinion of Newman within months, and it has been read ever since as autobiography by readers who share none of his conclusions. Historians of the Oxford Movement treat it as a primary source, and test it against his letters and diaries.

No. 31 of Lérins Newman, in its second part on the Catholic years 1848–1885, gives the 1865 text, from the Newman Reader transcription of the uniform edition in its 1908 impression. Newman’s preface on the provocation of 1864, his notes A to G and the supplemental letters and papers keep the form he gave them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the Kingsley controversy and on the difference between the editions of 1864 and 1865. Their explanatory notes identify the people, places, tracts, sermons and controversies that crowd the narrative, many of which Newman names in passing and expected his first readers to know.

title: The Dream of Gerontius
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s dramatic poem follows a dying man’s soul past death, through the mockery of demons and the praise of angels, to the judgment seat and the willing pain of purgatory.
description: The Dream of Gerontius was written in January 1865 and first published that spring in The Month, a Catholic magazine, before it appeared as a small book. It is a poem in seven sections. Gerontius, an old man, prays on his deathbed with his friends and a priest, and dies. His soul wakes in a strange stillness and finds itself carried by his guardian Angel. They pass the demons, who jeer at the saints, and the choirs of Angelicals, whose hymn begins “Praise to the Holiest in the height.” The Angel of the Agony pleads for the soul, which sees God for an instant and asks to be taken away and made clean. The poem ends with the souls in purgatory and the Angel’s farewell, “Softly and gently, dearly-ransom’d soul.”

The poem gives verse to Catholic teaching on death, the particular judgment and purgatory, and it treats purgatory as the soul’s own wish to be made fit for the sight of God. Its forms range from the litanies of the deathbed to blank verse dialogue and the strict stanzas of the choirs. It was widely read in Newman’s lifetime, and General Gordon kept a marked copy with him at Khartoum. Two of its passages, “Praise to the Holiest in the height” and “Firmly I believe and truly,” entered the hymn books of Catholic and Anglican churches alike. Edward Elgar’s setting of the poem as an oratorio, first performed in Birmingham in 1900, brought it to concert audiences and is still how many people first meet it.

No. 32 of Lérins Newman, in the collection’s second part on the Catholic years 1848–1885, sets the poem from the Newman Reader transcription of the text Newman included in his Verses on Various Occasions, and keeps his own notes as he left them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the writing of the poem, its theology and its later life in music. Their explanatory notes cover the prayers for the dying, the Latin of the deathbed and the choirs, and the scriptural and patristic sources behind its picture of judgment, so that the reader can follow the liturgy the poem assumes.

title: An Essay in Aid of a Grammar of Assent
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s study of belief asks how ordinary people come to be certain of things they cannot prove by strict logic, and finds the answer in the mind’s own power of judging, which he calls the illative sense.
description: An Essay in Aid of a Grammar of Assent was published in 1870, after many years in which Newman had tried and failed to write a book on faith and reason. He found his starting point in the summer of 1866, at Glion above Lake Geneva. The book has ten chapters in two parts. The first, on assent and apprehension, distinguishes the ways of holding a proposition, notional and real apprehension, and notional and real assent, and applies them to belief in one God, in the Holy Trinity and in dogmatic theology. The second, on assent and inference, treats simple and complex assent, certitude, formal, informal and natural inference, the illative sense, and inference and assent in natural and revealed religion. Newman dedicated it to his friend Edward Bellasis, Serjeant at Law.

Newman’s question is how a person can rightly be certain where the evidence falls short of demonstration, as it does in most of life and in religion. His answer is that reasoning in concrete matters works by the convergence of many probabilities, too many and too fine to be set out in a syllogism, and that the mind weighs them by a trained faculty of judgment, the illative sense. He sets real assent, given to things imagined and felt, against notional assent, given to abstractions. The book drew criticism in his lifetime, among others from Fairbairn, who read it as sceptical, and it has since been studied by philosophers of religion and of knowledge as well as by theologians. It is the most sustained piece of philosophy Newman wrote.

No. 33 of Lérins Newman, in the second part of the collection, the Catholic years 1848–1885, follows the Newman Reader transcription of the uniform edition in its 1903 impression. The dedication, Newman’s three closing notes on Hooker and Chillingworth, on the choice between atheism and Catholicity and on eternal punishment, and his footnotes all appear as he left them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the book’s long making and its reception, and explanatory notes on the philosophers, divines and examples Newman uses, from Aristotle and Locke to Butler and Paley, with guidance through the terms he coins.

title: A Letter to the Duke of Norfolk
author: John Henry Newman
lead: When Gladstone charged that Catholics after the Vatican Council could not be fully loyal subjects, Newman answered with an account of papal authority, its limits and the rights of conscience.
description: A Letter to the Duke of Norfolk was published in January 1875 as a reply to W. E. Gladstone’s pamphlet on the Vatican Decrees of 1870, which held that a convert to Rome now placed “his loyalty and civil duty at the mercy of another.” Newman addressed the letter, at a friend’s suggestion, to the Duke of Norfolk, hereditary Earl Marshal of England and the leading Catholic layman of the country. Its ten chapters move from introductory remarks through the ancient Church, the papal Church and divided allegiance to a chapter on conscience, then to the Encyclical of 1864, the Syllabus, the Vatican Council and the Vatican Definition, and a conclusion. A postscript dated 26 February 1875 answers Gladstone’s second pamphlet.

Newman’s case is that the Pope’s authority is real but bounded, that the Vatican definition of infallibility is narrow in its terms and must be read by the ordinary rules of theology, and that no papal command can bind a person to act against conscience. The chapter on conscience calls it “the aboriginal Vicar of Christ,” and ends with the after-dinner toast he would drink “to Conscience first, and to the Pope afterwards.” The letter was read widely in England on its appearance. It remains the fullest statement of Newman’s views on conscience and on papal authority, and it is quoted by writers of very different opinions, inside and outside the Catholic Church, on what the Vatican Council did and did not define.

No. 34 of Lérins Newman, in the collection’s second part, the Catholic years 1848–1885, sets the letter from the Newman Reader transcription of the second volume of Certain Difficulties Felt by Anglicans in Catholic Teaching, where Newman reprinted it, in the 1900 impression of the uniform edition. The dedication to the Duke, the postscript and Newman’s notes appear as he left them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on Gladstone’s pamphlets, the Vatican Council and the English debate over civil allegiance. Their explanatory notes identify the papal documents, councils, theologians and historical cases Newman cites, from the ancient Church to the Syllabus of 1864.

title: Five Letters
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Five letters of 1875 from Newman to his nephew, a young Cambridge fellow who had asked how the record of the Church in history could be squared with its claim to divine promises.
description: The letters gathered as Five Letters were written in 1875 to John Rickards Mozley, the son of Newman’s sister Jemima and a fellow of King’s College, Cambridge. Mozley had put questions to his uncle about the moral record of the Church of Rome, pointing to Spain under Philip II, France up to the Revolution and Italy into the nineteenth century, and asking how a body to which divine promises were believed to have been entrusted could show such conduct. Newman answered in letters dated 1 April, 4 April, 21 April and 16 May, and a last one of 3 December 1875. Mozley printed them after his uncle’s death, in The Contemporary Review for September 1899, with an introduction of his own setting out the questions they answer, which this volume keeps.

The letters are Newman’s private answer to an objection he usually met in public. He says his reply will take the shape of accounting for his own insensibility to the objections. He sets out the first principles he assumes, that there is truth in religion and that there is a God to whom we are responsible, admits that the existence of evil is a difficulty he cannot overcome, and argues that Christianity recognises that difficulty in the death of Christ. In the last letter he holds that the difference between Catholics and Protestants is at bottom ethical. The tone is patient and affectionate. Read with the Grammar of Assent of five years before, the letters show its account of belief applied to a single, personal case.

No. 35 of Lérins Newman, in the second part of the collection, the Catholic years 1848–1885, sets the letters from the Newman Reader transcription of their first printing in The Contemporary Review of September 1899, together with Mozley’s introduction, and keeps Newman’s notes as he left them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the Mozley family, Newman’s relations with his sisters and their children, and the questions of 1875. Their explanatory notes cover the historical cases Mozley raised, the theological terms Newman uses and the books and events to which the correspondence refers.

title: Select Treatises of St. Athanasius, Volume 1
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s own translation of the treatises in which Athanasius defended the Council of Nicaea against the Arians, made for the Oxford Library of the Fathers and revised by him as a Catholic in 1881.
description: Select Treatises of St. Athanasius, Volume 1 holds Newman’s English version of four documents of the Arian controversy. It opens with the encyclical letter of Alexander, Archbishop of Alexandria, on his deposition and excommunication of Arius, which Newman thought Athanasius drafted as his bishop’s secretary. Then come the Epistle in Defence of the Nicene Definition of the Homoüsion, with the letter of Eusebius of Cæsarea to the people of his diocese, and the Epistle on the Councils held at Ariminum in Italy and at Seleucia in Isauria. The volume closes with the three Discourses against the Arians. Each work has Newman’s prefatory notice and a running commentary in his footnotes. He had first translated these treatises in 1841–1844 for Pusey’s Library of the Fathers, and he revised the translation in 1881 for his collected works, omitting the so-called Fourth Discourse.

Athanasius was bishop of Alexandria for most of the years from 328 to 373 and was exiled five times for his defence of the faith of Nicaea. These treatises are the core of his case that the Son is of one substance with the Father, and they are basic texts for the history of the doctrine of the Trinity in every tradition that keeps the Nicene Creed. For Newman they were more than a scholarly task. His study of the Arian crisis had produced his first book, The Arians of the Fourth Century, and fed the thinking he later traced in the Apologia. In the revision of 1881 he relaxed the strict literalism the Oxford translators had practised, so that the English reads more freely while keeping close to the Greek.

No. 36 of Lérins Newman, in its second part on the Catholic years 1848–1885, sets the text from the Newman Reader transcription of the uniform edition’s 1903 impression of the revised translation. Newman’s prefatory notices and his footnotes, which form a commentary in their own right, are kept as he left them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on Athanasius, the councils of the fourth century and Newman’s work as translator over forty years, and explanatory notes on the persons, creeds and Greek terms of the controversy. The companion volume of Newman’s annotations is No. 37.

title: Select Treatises of St. Athanasius, Volume 2
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The second volume of Newman’s Athanasius is his own reference book to the Arian controversy, a series of short articles on its persons, doctrines and Greek terms, arranged in alphabetical order.
description: Select Treatises of St. Athanasius, Volume 2 contains no translation. It is a set of annotations on the treatises in Volume 1, arranged alphabetically in two series. The first takes theological subjects, among them Adam, the Arians, the Vicarious Atonement, the Coinherence, Deification, Economical Language, the Incarnation, the Blessed Mary, Private Judgment, the Rule of Faith, the Scripture Canon, Tradition and the Holy Trinity in Unity, with entries on figures such as Arius, Eusebius, Marcellus, Meletius, Paul of Samosata and Sabellius. The second takes Greek terms of the controversy, from agenneton and homoousios to ousia, monogenes, Logos and Theotokos. Much of this material grew out of the long notes Newman had attached to his Oxford translation of the 1840s, gathered into one place for the revised edition of 1881.

The volume is Newman’s most compact statement of patristic theology as he understood it at the end of his life. In short articles he sets out what Athanasius and the other Fathers meant by their key words, how the Nicene terms came to be fixed, and how the controversy bore on later questions of tradition, development and the rule of faith. The entries on Scripture and Tradition show his long interest in how doctrine is handed on. Scholarship on the Fathers has moved on since 1881 on many points of text and dating. The annotations remain a guide to the vocabulary of fourth-century theology, and to the way Newman himself read it after half a century of study.

No. 37 of Lérins Newman, the companion to No. 36 in the second part of the collection, the Catholic years 1848–1885, follows the Newman Reader transcription of the 1903 impression of the uniform edition. Newman’s articles, his cross-references and his Greek terms appear as he left them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the history of the annotations and on how to use them with the treatises, and explanatory notes that identify the Fathers, councils and heretics Newman cites and render his Greek and Latin terms for readers who do not have those languages.

title: On the Inspiration of Scripture
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s late essay asks what a Catholic is bound to believe about the Bible, and separates what the Church has defined about inspiration from the questions it has left open.
description: On the Inspiration of Scripture appeared in The Nineteenth Century in February 1884, when Newman was a cardinal in his eighties. It answers a charge, made in an English journal after Ernest Renan described how his study of the Bible had led him away from Catholicism, that the Church demands of converts an assent to readings of Scripture that science and history have discredited. Newman proposes to state what Catholics really hold and what a Catholic is bound to believe. He works from the decrees of the Councils of Florence, Trent and the Vatican, considers the Church’s office as interpreter, and asks whether Scripture may contain obiter dicta, statements made in passing that are not the matter of inspiration. He ends by submitting his remarks to the judgment of the Holy See.

The essay belongs to the debates that followed the rise of historical criticism, geology and evolutionary theory in the nineteenth century. Newman holds that the books of Scripture are inspired throughout in all matters of faith and morals and that the Church interprets them, and he asks how far that commitment extends to incidental statements of fact. His suggestion about obiter dicta was challenged by other Catholic writers, and the questions he raised were taken up in papal teaching with Leo XIII’s encyclical Providentissimus Deus of 1893. Historians of Catholic biblical study read the essay as an early attempt by a senior churchman to meet modern criticism directly, and it is still cited in discussion of how inspiration and error are to be understood.

No. 38 of Lérins Newman, in its second part on the Catholic years 1848–1885, gives the essay from the Newman Reader transcription of the article as it appeared in The Nineteenth Century, volume 15, February 1884, with its numbered paragraphs and with Newman’s notes as he left them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the Victorian argument over the Bible and on Catholic teaching about Scripture before and after 1884. Their explanatory notes cover the conciliar texts, the theologians and the critics Newman names, and the passages of Scripture he discusses.

title: The Development of Religious Error
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s last article, written at eighty-four, answers a Congregationalist scholar who had charged him with a hidden scepticism, and restates how reason, conscience and faith belong together in his thought.
description: The Development of Religious Error appeared in The Contemporary Review in October 1885. In May of that year Principal A. M. Fairbairn had published in the same review an article on Catholicism and religious thought, arguing that Newman’s defence of faith rested on an underlying philosophical scepticism, a distrust of reason that left authority to do its work. Newman replied briefly and directly. He denies the charge, explains the sense in which he uses the word reason, and protests at what he took to be the misreading of the Grammar of Assent. Near the start he adopts the words of Polycarp before his martyrdom, “For fourscore years and six I have served my Lord.” This volume adds the further sections Newman printed privately in 1890, on philosophical scepticism, the meaning of reason, its faculty and final causes.

The exchange tested, late in Newman’s life, the account of belief he had given in his Oxford University Sermons and in the Grammar of Assent. Fairbairn read his stress on conscience and on the limits of formal reasoning as scepticism. Newman answers that he had always held reason to be a true faculty, able to reach truth, and that his concern was with the way it works in actual minds under the guidance of other powers. Fairbairn replied in the review in December, and the sections of 1890 answer that reply point by point. The article is short, but it shows Newman defending his life’s work in his last years, and it is read with the Grammar by students of his theory of knowledge.

No. 39 of Lérins Newman, in the second part of the collection, the Catholic years 1848–1885, sets the October 1885 article from the Newman Reader transcription of The Contemporary Review, followed by the sections Newman appended in Stray Essays on Controversial Points, privately printed in 1890. His notes stand as he left them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on Fairbairn, the debate in the review and its place in Newman’s thought, and explanatory notes on the philosophers, the works of Newman under dispute and the passages each side quoted against the other.

title: Meditations and Devotions
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The prayers and meditations Newman wrote for his own use and for his community, gathered after his death, including the meditation on God creating each person for “some definite service.”
description: Meditations and Devotions was edited in 1893 by Father William P. Neville, Newman’s secretary in his last years, from papers that Newman had meant in part for a “Year-Book of Devotion” he never completed. The book is dedicated to the boys of the Oratory School. It has three parts. The first holds meditations on the Litany of Loretto for the month of May, arranged under the Immaculate Conception, the Annunciation, Our Lady’s Dolours and the Assumption, with a memorandum on the Immaculate Conception and a novena and litany of St. Philip Neri. The second gives meditations on the Stations of the Cross, twelve meditations and intercessions for Good Friday, meditations for eight days and a series of litanies. The third is a set of meditations on Christian doctrine, with a short visit to the Blessed Sacrament.

These pages show Newman praying rather than arguing. The Marian meditations are short readings for each day of May. The meditations on Christian doctrine, on hope in God, on God and the soul, on sin, on the Holy Ghost and on the Sacred Heart, are written in the first person and addressed to God. The meditation on hope in God as Creator says that “God has created me to do Him some definite service,” and it has become one of the most quoted passages Newman wrote. The prayers have been used by Catholics and by readers of other traditions since the book appeared. The volume gives the inner life behind the public controversies of his Catholic years, in his own voice.

No. 40 of Lérins Newman, in its second part, the Catholic years 1848–1885, takes its text from the Newman Reader transcription of Neville’s edition in the 1907 impression, with his dedication and prefatory notice. Newman’s own notes, and the few added by his first editor, are kept as they were left. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the papers, what can be known of their dates and Neville’s work in arranging them. Their explanatory notes cover the litanies, feasts and Latin texts the meditations use and the devotions of the Oratory that they assume.

title: Faith and Prejudice, and Other Sermons
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Nine sermons Newman wrote out as a Catholic that went unpublished in his lifetime, seven of them from his first weeks of preaching in Birmingham in 1848.
description: Faith and Prejudice, and Other Sermons was edited by the Birmingham Oratory and first published in 1956. Its introduction explains that of the sermons Newman composed as a Catholic whose autographs survive, only these nine seem to have escaped publication. Seven were preached at St. Chad’s Cathedral, Birmingham, in the early months of 1848, when Newman was living at Maryvale and walked in to preach, the last of them on the third Sunday of Lent. They include “The Omnipotence of God the Reason for Faith and Hope,” “Preparation for the Judgment,” “Prejudice and Faith,” “Surrender to God” and “Our Lady in the Gospel.” The eighth, “Stewards and also Sons of God,” dates from July 1870, and the ninth, “The Infidelity of the Future,” from the opening of St. Bernard’s Seminary at Olton in October 1873.

The 1848 sermons are among the first Newman preached in England as a Catholic priest, weeks after his return from Rome, and they show him speaking to a Catholic congregation in a manufacturing town for the first time. He wrote them out in full and numbered them, as he had done as an Anglican, and they treat the themes of his Oxford pulpit, faith, judgment, grace and the world, from his new position. “The Infidelity of the Future” is the best known. Preached to seminarians, it warns that the coming age will face unbelief of a kind the Church has not met before, and it is often quoted for what the introduction calls its “grim forecast of the future course of unbelief.”

No. 41 of Lérins Newman closes the second part of the collection, the Catholic years 1848–1885. The text follows the Newman Reader transcription of the Birmingham Oratory’s 1956 edition, with its introduction on the manuscripts and the occasions, and with Newman’s own notes as he left them. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction placing the sermons in the founding of the English Oratory and in the Catholic Birmingham of 1848 and 1873. Their explanatory notes cover the Scripture, the liturgical seasons and the persons the sermons name, and compare passages with the Anglican sermons on the same themes.

title: Froude’s Remains
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Richard Hurrell Froude died at thirty-two and left his private journal and letters to his friends. Newman and John Keble chose to print them, and wrote this preface to say why they had.
description: Richard Hurrell Froude, Fellow and Tutor of Oriel College, died of consumption in the parsonage at Dartington in Devon on 28 February 1836. He left a large body of writing, none of it prepared for the press. John Henry Newman and John Keble edited a selection as the Remains of the Late Reverend Richard Hurrell Froude, and the first two volumes appeared in 1838. Their Preface, dated the Feast of the Purification 1838, is the text of this book. It sets out Froude’s life in brief, from Eton and Oriel to the winters he spent in the south of Europe and the West Indies. It lists what the volumes hold, the Journal, the Occasional Thoughts, an Essay on Fiction, sermons and letters. And it defends the decision to print a private journal and private letters at all.

The editors rest their case on the cause Froude served. They argue that his papers were a witness to Catholic views he had given his short life to, and that this alone justified disclosures his family and friends would otherwise have kept back. They answer in advance the reader startled by Froude’s self-condemnation, the critic who will find in the volumes a tendency toward Romanism, and the complaint that the letters are padded with small details. The Remains did become a centre of controversy. Froude’s candid remarks on the English Reformers were quoted against the Oxford Movement for years afterward. The Preface is the editors’ own account of what they meant by publishing him, written before that storm broke.

This is No. 42 of Lérins Newman, the first title in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. The Preface was written jointly by the two editors, so it is Newman’s only in part, and it is presented here as the work of both. Froude’s own journal, letters and sermons are not reprinted. The text is set from the NewmanReader transcription held in the site’s library, taken from the first volume of 1838. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on Froude, the making of the Remains and the dispute that followed, with explanatory notes on the people and events the Preface touches. The original editors’ wording and notes are kept as they left them.

title: Hymni Ecclesiae
author: John Henry Newman
lead: A book of Latin office hymns that Newman drew from the breviaries of Paris, Rome, Salisbury and York, with his English preface on why hymns are the hardest form of praise to write.
description: Hymni Ecclesiae is a collection of Latin hymns of the Divine Office that John Henry Newman edited in two parts. Part I takes its hymns from the Paris Breviary, and Newman’s English Preface to it is signed and dated 21 February 1838. Part II draws on the Roman, Sarum and York breviaries and other sources, and carries a short Latin Praefatio, also signed with his initials. The two parts were issued together in London in 1865. In the first Preface Newman explains his choice. He kept only hymns for the holy days and seasons recognized by the Church of England, or for events recorded in Scripture, and left out those whose invocations of the saints he judged to be supplications rather than apostrophes.

The Preface is a short essay on what a hymn is. Newman sets hymns beside the Psalms and Canticles, which are inspired, and argues that hymns, as direct addresses to God, are the hardest of the three to write well. He notes that the English Reformers set aside the Roman hymns and put a metrical psalter in their place. He holds that the old hymns were the gradual work of many generations, not the outpouring of one mind, and that even the newer Parisian hymns breathe an ancient spirit. The book belongs to the years of Tract 75, on the Roman Breviary, when Newman and his friends were turning to the breviary for English devotion. The Latin Praefatio makes the same plea in brief, asking the reader to weigh the old hymns with judgment rather than reject them whole.

This is No. 43 of Lérins Newman, in the part given to collected essays, sketches and verse. What is Newman’s here is the selection and his two prefaces. The hymns themselves are the work of many hands across the centuries, from the medieval offices to the French breviary of the eighteenth century. The text follows the NewmanReader transcription in the site’s library, made from the 1865 edition, which holds the English Preface of 1838, the Latin Praefatio and the title page. The Editors of Mere Catholicity supply a new introduction on the book and the breviaries behind it, with explanatory notes, and Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them.

title: The Library of the Fathers
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman was one of the three editors of the Oxford Library of the Fathers. These are the prefaces he wrote for its volumes of Cyril of Jerusalem, Cyprian of Carthage and John Chrysostom.
description: The Library of the Fathers was a series of English translations of the early Church writers, begun at Oxford in 1838 under the editorship of Edward Bouverie Pusey, John Keble and John Henry Newman, and dedicated to William Howley, Archbishop of Canterbury. This book gathers the dedication and three prefaces that Newman wrote and signed for the series. The first introduces the Catechetical Lectures of St. Cyril of Jerusalem, given to candidates for baptism beside the place of the crucifixion. The second, dated from Oxford on the Feast of St. Mark 1839, introduces the Treatises of St. Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage and martyr. The third introduces St. John Chrysostom’s Commentary on the Epistle to the Galatians and his Homilies on the Epistle to the Ephesians.

The Cyril preface is the longest and the fullest. It places Cyril in the divided church politics of the fourth century, where he did not receive justice from his contemporaries, and then turns to a question that occupied Newman throughout these years, how the Fathers stand to Scripture. His answer is that they declare doctrine and say that it is in Scripture, rather than prove it from Scripture text by text. The Cyprian preface discusses the text of the treatises and the Latin Bible Cyprian quotes. The Chrysostom preface dates the homilies from their own evidence. Together the prefaces state the purpose of the series, to set the early Church before English readers in its own words, and they record Newman’s thinking on tradition at the height of the Oxford Movement.

This is No. 44 of Lérins Newman, among its collected essays, sketches and verse. Only the prefaces are Newman’s. The translations they introduced were made by others, and the prefaces themselves thank R. W. Church for the Cyril, Charles Thornton for the Cyprian, and William John Copeland for the Ephesians homilies. The text is set from the NewmanReader transcription in the site’s library, with the Cyril preface from the fourth edition of 1872 and the other two from the volumes of 1840. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the Library and Newman’s part in it, with explanatory notes on the Fathers and editions he cites. Newman’s own notes stand as he left them.

title: Historical Tracts of St. Athanasius
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The papers Athanasius gathered to defend himself against the Arians, from the letters of councils and popes to the soldiers breaking into his church, edited by Newman for the Oxford Library of the Fathers.
description: Historical Tracts of St. Athanasius was published at Oxford in 1843 as a volume of the Library of the Fathers, with a preface signed by John Henry Newman on 4 December of that year. It gathers eight works of Athanasius, Archbishop of Alexandria. They are the Encyclical Epistle, the Apology against the Arians with its documents from the Council of Egypt, Pope Julius, the Council of Sardica and the Council of Tyre, the Encyclical to the Bishops of Egypt and Libya, the Apology to the Emperor Constantius, the Apology for his Flight, the letter to Serapion on the death of Arius, the letter to the Monks, and the History of the Arians, whose opening is lost.

These tracts are a chief first-hand record of the Arian controversy in the decades after Nicaea. In them Athanasius answers the charges laid against him by the Meletians and at Tyre, prints the letters that cleared him, and tells how he was driven from Alexandria again and again. The Apology for his Flight describes the soldiers of Duke Syrianus breaking into the Church of Theonas while he sat on his throne there. Newman’s preface is a long study of the chronology of the period, which he warns can be no more than hypothetical, beginning with the intervention of Pope Julius in the affairs of the East. Newman had written on the Arians since 1833, and Athanasius remained central to his work for the rest of his life.

This is No. 45 of Lérins Newman, in the part for collected essays, sketches and verse. Newman edited the volume and wrote its preface. The English translation itself is acknowledged in that preface to the Rev. Miles Atkinson, late Fellow of Lincoln College, and is given here as the work of both men in their parts. The text is set from the NewmanReader transcription of the 1843 volume in the site’s library. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction to the tracts, their history and Newman’s work on them, with explanatory notes on persons, councils and dates. The notes of the 1843 edition are kept as they were left.

title: Verses on Various Occasions
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s collected poems, from verses written at sea in 1833 to The Dream of Gerontius, with Lead, Kindly Light among them under the title he gave it, The Pillar of the Cloud.
description: Verses on Various Occasions is the collection of his poems that John Henry Newman published in 1868, dedicated from the Oratory on 21 December 1867 to his friend Edward Badeley. The poems are numbered and broadly arranged by date. Early pieces include Solitude, My Birthday and Snapdragon. Many were written during the Mediterranean voyage of 1832 and 1833, among them The Pillar of the Cloud, dated At Sea, June 16, 1833, which begins “Lead, Kindly Light, amid the encircling gloom.” The Catholic poems include translations of breviary hymns for the hours, poems on St. Philip Neri written at the Oratory, and The Dream of Gerontius, dated January 1865. Appendices give Latin verse, among them prologues for plays.

In the dedication Newman calls these poems effusions he had always thought ephemeral, and says he gathered them only because critics had begun to praise them. He says too that a chief portion of the volume grew out of the religious movement he and Badeley had followed together, and he thanks Badeley for his legal help in the matter in which, as he puts it, he found himself in collision with the law of the land, the Achilli trial. The voyage poems record the months before the Oxford Movement began, and several first appeared in the Lyra Apostolica. The Dream of Gerontius follows a soul from its deathbed to judgment. Lead, Kindly Light passed into the hymnbooks of many traditions, and Elgar set Gerontius to music in 1900.

This is No. 46 of Lérins Newman, the one book of verse in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. Every poem in it is Newman’s, either his own composition or his translation, as with the breviary hymns and the passages from St. Gregory Nazianzen. The text is set from the NewmanReader transcription of the 1868 collection held in the site’s library, with Newman’s dates and places at the foot of the poems. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction to the poems and the occasions behind them, and explanatory notes on names, places and allusions. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them.

title: Essays Critical and Historical, Volume 1
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Nine essays from Newman’s Oxford years, on poetry, rationalism, tradition and the prospects of the English Church, reprinted by him in 1871 with notes on where his mind had since changed.
description: Essays Critical and Historical, Volume 1, opens the two volumes in which John Henry Newman collected his longer articles in 1871, with a dedication to William Froude dated 1 August 1871. It begins with Poetry, with reference to Aristotle’s Poetics, written in 1828 for the London Review. Tract 73, On the Introduction of Rationalistic Principles into Revealed Religion, follows, with its discussion of Thomas Erskine and of Jacob Abbott’s Corner Stone. The rest are reviews from the British Critic of 1836 to 1840. They are Apostolical Tradition, the Fall of de la Mennais, Palmer on Faith and Unity, the Theology of St. Ignatius, Prospects of the Anglican Church, the Anglo-American Church, and Selina, Countess of Huntingdon.

The essays show Newman at work as a leading writer of the Oxford Movement, setting the Church of England’s claim to be part of the Catholic Church against its history and its critics. They take up the authority of tradition, the danger he saw in judging revelation by private reason, and the fortunes of other bodies, from de la Mennais in France to the Episcopal Church in America. In 1871 Newman, by then a Catholic, chose to reprint them without alteration rather than leave others to reprint them without comment. His Advertisement explains the plan, and the notes he added to several essays answer what he no longer held. A reader therefore has his first thoughts and his second side by side.

This is No. 47 of Lérins Newman, and the first of the two volumes of Essays Critical and Historical in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. The text follows the NewmanReader transcription of the 1871 edition in the site’s library, with the dedication, the Advertisement and the later notes in their places. The Editors of Mere Catholicity contribute a new introduction placing each essay in the years from 1828 to 1840, and explanatory notes on the books reviewed and the persons named. Newman’s own notes, early and late, are kept as he left them, so that both layers of his text remain visible.

title: Essays Critical and Historical, Volume 2
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The last of Newman’s Anglican journalism, from the British Critic of 1840 to 1842, together with his Catholic review of Keble’s Lyra Innocentium and the notes he added in 1871.
description: Essays Critical and Historical, Volume 2, continues the collection John Henry Newman made in 1871. Six of its seven essays first appeared in the British Critic between January 1840 and April 1842. They are the Catholicity of the Anglican Church, the Protestant Idea of Antichrist, Milman’s View of Christianity, the Reformation of the Eleventh Century, Private Judgment, and a study of John Davison, the Oriel divine. The seventh, John Keble, is a review of Keble’s Lyra Innocentium dated June 1846, written after Newman had become a Catholic. A Postscript prints William Palmer of Worcester College’s disavowal of opinions that Newman had ascribed to him in the first volume.

The Catholicity of the Anglican Church, of January 1840, is the fullest statement in these volumes of the claim that the English Church is a true part of the Catholic Church despite its separation from Rome. The Antichrist essay argues against the Protestant reading of the Pope as Antichrist. The review of Milman, the essay on the reforming popes of the eleventh century and the essay on Private Judgment take up how Christian doctrine grows and on what authority belief rests. The notes Newman added in 1871 set his later judgment beside his earlier argument. The volume records the period in which, by his own account, his Anglican position gave way, and it is read both as Anglican apologetic and as a stage on the road to the Essay on Development.

This is No. 48 of Lérins Newman, the second volume of Essays Critical and Historical within its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. Newman’s text is set from the NewmanReader transcription of the 1871 edition held in the site’s library, keeping the dates of first publication at the head of each essay. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the essays and the years 1840 to 1846, and explanatory notes on the authors, controversies and historical figures they discuss. Newman’s own notes, including those he wrote as a Catholic, stand as he left them, and the Postscript closes the volume as he placed it.

title: Tracts Theological and Ecclesiastical
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s technical studies of the early Church, from Latin dissertations on Athanasius written in Rome in 1847 to the causes of Arianism, the Ignatian letters, Cyril’s formula and the Douay Bible.
description: Tracts Theological and Ecclesiastical gathers seven studies written by John Henry Newman over more than forty years, in a volume whose Advertisement is dated from Birmingham on 5 January 1874. It opens with four Latin dissertations, among them one on the fourth Oration of St. Athanasius against the Arians and two on the anathemas of Nicaea, dedicated to Antonio Bresciani, Rector of the Collegio Urbano in Rome. Then come an essay on the text of the seven Epistles of St. Ignatius, begun in notes of 1828 and completed in 1870, a long study of the causes of the rise and successes of Arianism, the Heresy of Apollinaris from notes of 1835, and St. Cyril’s formula from the Atlantis of 1858. The volume closes with the Ordo de Tempore in the Roman Breviary and the history of the text of the Rheims and Douay Bible.

Much of the book is close scholarship on texts and terms. The Ignatius essay defends the substantial genuineness of the seven letters against the case built on the shorter Syriac text that William Cureton published in 1845. The study of Arianism traces the tradition of the doctrine of the Holy Trinity before Nicaea, and the openings that early ways of speaking, such as the principatus of the Father and the temporal gennesis of the Son, gave to heresy. The Apollinaris and Cyril essays turn to the doctrine of the Incarnation. The volume shows the patristic learning behind Newman’s better known books, from The Arians of the Fourth Century to the Essay on Development, and its later pieces apply that learning to the Catholic liturgy and the English Catholic Bible.

This is No. 49 of Lérins Newman, part of its collected essays, sketches and verse. The text is set from the NewmanReader transcription of the 1874 collection in the site’s library, with Newman’s Advertisement, his list of the editions of the Fathers he used, and his corrigenda. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction that sets each tract in its time and controversy, and explanatory notes that identify the Fathers, councils and modern critics Newman cites and gloss the Greek and Latin terms on which his arguments turn. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them, in the languages he wrote them in.

title: Discussions and Arguments on Various Subjects
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Six pieces from 1836 to 1866, among them Newman’s Tract lectures on Antichrist and on Scripture and the Creed, and his letters to the Times answering Sir Robert Peel on the Tamworth Reading Room.
description: Discussions and Arguments on Various Subjects is a volume John Henry Newman issued in January 1872 toward the uniform edition of his works, dedicated to his old Oxford friend Henry Arthur Woodgate. It holds six pieces. How to Accomplish It is a discussion between two Anglicans, first printed in the British Magazine in 1836 as Home Thoughts Abroad. The Patristical Idea of Antichrist and Holy Scripture in its Relation to the Catholic Creed are Tracts 83 and 85, published in 1838. The Tamworth Reading Room appeared in the Times in February 1841 over the name Catholicus. Who’s to Blame? is a set of letters written in the spring of 1855 for the Catholic Standard. An Internal Argument for Christianity is a review from the Month of June 1866.

The Tamworth Reading Room is the best known piece. Peel, opening a library and reading room at Tamworth, had spoken as if secular knowledge could make men morally better and bind society together. Newman answers in seven letters, whose headings carry the argument. Secular knowledge, they say, is not the principle, the means or the antecedent of moral improvement, nor a principle of social unity or of action, and without personal religion it tends to unbelief. The lectures on Scripture and the Creed compare the difficulties of proving the Creed from Scripture with the difficulties of the canon itself. Who’s to Blame? studies the British constitution at a time of national strain by setting the character of Englishmen beside that of the Athenians.

This is No. 50 of Lérins Newman, within its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. Newman’s text is set from the NewmanReader transcription of the 1872 edition in the site’s library, with his Advertisement on the origin of each piece. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction to the six pieces and their occasions, from the Tracts for the Times to the Crimean War and the Catholic press of the 1860s, and explanatory notes on the persons, books and public events Newman answers. Newman’s own notes stand as he left them, including the brackets he added when he reprinted the pieces.

title: Historical Sketches, Volume 1
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s lectures of 1853 on the history of the Turks, given as Russia and Turkey moved toward war, with his early encyclopedia articles on Cicero and Apollonius of Tyana and his Anglican papers on primitive Christianity.
description: Historical Sketches, Volume 1, is the first of three volumes in which John Henry Newman gathered his historical writing in 1872, dedicated on 23 October of that year to David Moriarty, Bishop of Kerry. Most of it is taken up by nine lectures on the history of the Turks in its relation to Christianity, given in 1853 when the collision between Russia and Turkey was, as the first lecture says, engaging public attention. They run from the tribes of the north and the Tartars, through the Turk and the Saracen and the Pope and the Turk, to the past, present and future of the Ottomans. Then come two articles written for the Encyclopaedia Metropolitana, on Marcus Tullius Cicero and on Apollonius of Tyana, and five chapters on primitive Christianity that ask what St. Ambrose, Vincent of Lerins and the Apostolical Canons say.

The Turkish lectures weigh barbarism against civilization and ask what the past of the Ottomans implied for their future, with chronological tables for the general reader. The encyclopedia articles are among Newman’s earliest published prose. The life of Cicero follows the orator through Roman politics, and the piece on Apollonius argues against the attempt, made in the early centuries and revived in England, to set the Pythagorean wonder-worker up as a rival to Christ. The papers on primitive Christianity, which the dedication calls the work of an Anglican controversialist, use the lives of Ambrose and his contemporaries to show the Church of the fourth century in practice. Together they show the range of Newman’s historical reading across three decades.

This is No. 51 of Lérins Newman, the first of the three volumes of Historical Sketches in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. The text is set from the NewmanReader transcription of the 1872 collection held in the site’s library, with the notes and chronological tables of the Turkish lectures. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the three groups of writings and their dates, and explanatory notes on the peoples, rulers and places that a modern reader may not know. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them, including the classical references of the Cicero and Apollonius articles.

title: Historical Sketches, Volume 2
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Portraits of the Fathers drawn from their own letters and lives, Basil and Gregory, Antony, Augustine, Martin, Chrysostom and Theodoret, with Newman’s two essays on St. Benedict and the Benedictine schools.
description: Historical Sketches, Volume 2, gathers John Henry Newman’s studies of the early and early medieval Church. The largest part is The Church of the Fathers, papers which, as the Advertisement says, appeared with two or three exceptions in the British Magazine from 1833, and which were dedicated to Isaac Williams in February 1840. Its chapters treat the trials and labours of Basil, Basil and Gregory, the rise and fall of Gregory, Antony in conflict and in calm, Augustine and the Vandals, the Conversion of Augustine, Demetrias, and Martin and Maximus. The volume adds St. Chrysostom, from the Rambler of 1859, the Trials of Theodoret, and two essays from the Atlantis of 1858 and 1859, The Mission of St. Benedict and The Benedictine Schools.

Newman’s aim in The Church of the Fathers was to show the tone, habits and manners of the early Church through its saints, often in their own words, which he translated at length. The Conversion of Augustine retells the scene in the garden at Milan from the Confessions. The St. Chrysostom chapters follow the bishop from Constantinople to exile and death, and the Theodoret study traces the Bishop of Cyrrhus from his monastic youth through the Council of Ephesus to his last years. The Benedictine essays, written for the Catholic University’s journal, describe the monks as patient restorers of land and learning after the fall of Rome. The papers come partly from Newman’s Anglican years and partly from his Catholic ones, and here the two sit side by side.

This is No. 52 of Lérins Newman, the second volume of Historical Sketches in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. Newman’s text is set from the NewmanReader transcription of the 1872 collection in the site’s library, with the dedication to Isaac Williams, the Advertisement and the chronology of contemporary events. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the papers and their first readers, and explanatory notes on the saints, places and ancient sources Newman draws on. His own notes and translations stand as he left them, and the order of the papers is his.

title: Historical Sketches, Volume 3
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s sketch of what a university is and how universities grew, written in Dublin in 1854, with his essays on the Northmen and Normans, on medieval Oxford and on the Convocation of Canterbury.
description: Historical Sketches, Volume 3, opens with The Rise and Progress of Universities, twenty chapters that first appeared in 1854 in the Dublin Catholic University Gazette, while John Henry Newman was Rector of the new Catholic University of Ireland. They were published in 1856 as Office and Work of Universities, dedicated from Dublin to James Hope Scott, and given their present title in 1872. The chapters run from What is a University? and the site of a university to student life at Athens, the Sophists, the Lombards, the isles of the north, the schools of Charlemagne, the schoolmen, Abelard, and the colleges of Oxford. The volume adds The Northmen and Normans in England and Ireland from the Rambler of 1859, Medieval Oxford from the British Critic of 1838, and five chapters on the Convocation of Canterbury.

The university chapters are lighter in manner than the Dublin discourses that became The Idea of a University. Newman wrote them, as the Advertisement says, under a profession of incognito and in a conversational tone, and kept both when he reprinted them. Their recurring point is that a university lives by the personal influence of teachers on students, and that colleges are the corrective that discipline a university’s breadth. He draws it from Athens, from the medieval schools and from Oxford, which he knew from within. The Northmen essay treats the Danes and Normans in the history of the Church in England and Ireland. The Convocation chapters examine the constitution of the ancient synod of the province of Canterbury, its two houses, and its relation to the Crown.

This is No. 53 of Lérins Newman, and the last of the three volumes of Historical Sketches in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. The text is set from the NewmanReader transcription of the 1872 collection held in the site’s library, with Newman’s dedication of 1856 and his Advertisement. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the Dublin university and on the other papers gathered here, and explanatory notes on the scholars, schools and institutions Newman names. Newman’s own notes are kept as he left them, and the bracketed notes of first publication stand at the head of the later papers.

title: The Church and the Empires
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Newman’s memoir of his Oriel pupil and lifelong friend Henry Wilberforce, whose parsonage took in the priests and nuns nursing cholera among the hop pickers of 1849, and who became a Catholic a year later.
description: The Church and the Empires is a book of historical essays by Henry William Wilberforce, published in London in 1874, the year after his death. John Henry Newman wrote the memoir that opens it, signed with his initials and dated 14 July 1873, and that memoir is the text of this book. It follows Wilberforce from his birth at Clapham in 1807, the youngest son of William Wilberforce, through Oriel, where Newman read with him as private tutor in the long vacations, to his three parishes at Bransgore, Walmer and East Farleigh. It then tells of his reception into the Catholic Church on 15 September 1850, his years as a Catholic editor, a winter in Jamaica for his health, and his death on 23 April 1873.

The memoir is a portrait of a friendship of nearly fifty years. Newman describes the small and timid freshman of 1826, the President of the Union who restored order to a wrecked debate with one question, “Has the noble Lord no friends here?”, and the parson who brought daily service into each of his churches. Its turning point is the autumn of 1849, when cholera broke out among the Irish hop pickers at East Farleigh and Wilberforce took into his parsonage the Fathers of the London Oratory and the nuns of the Good Shepherd who came to nurse them. Newman presents the conversion that followed as the work of a clear mind and a strong sense of the unseen world, and records his later editing of the Catholic Standard and the Weekly Register.

This is No. 54 of Lérins Newman, in the part given to collected essays, sketches and verse. What is Newman’s here is the Memoir. Wilberforce’s own essays, which fill the rest of the 1874 volume, are not reprinted. The text is set from the NewmanReader transcription of the Memoir held in the site’s library. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on Wilberforce, his family and his long friendship with Newman, and explanatory notes on the people, places and Oxford events the Memoir names. Newman’s own wording, and any notes he left, are kept as they stand in the original.

title: Notes of a Visit to the Russian Church
author: William Palmer, edited by John Henry Newman
lead: In 1840 an Oxford fellow went to Russia to ask the Orthodox Church for communion as his right. William Palmer’s journal of that visit was put into shape by Newman from the papers Palmer left him.
description: Notes of a Visit to the Russian Church is the journal of William Palmer, Fellow of Magdalen College, Oxford, of his first visit to Russia, made in 1840 and 1841. Palmer, a brother of Lord Chancellor Selborne, went to seek admission to the sacraments of the Russian Church as an Anglican. He was received into the Catholic Church in 1855 and died at Rome on 5 April 1879, leaving all his papers by will to John Henry Newman. Newman selected and arranged the journal, with help from Father Eaglesim of the Birmingham Oratory, and published it in 1882 with a Prefatory Notice dated Easter of that year. The Notice explains Palmer’s purpose, tells how the book came to be made, and adds the principal dates of his life.

Palmer held what Newman calls the formal teaching of Anglicanism at Oxford in those years, that the one Church existed in three branches, Latin, Greek and Anglican, so that an Anglican in Russia had a claim to communion there. The journal records how the Synod and clergy of Petersburg met that claim. They received him with courtesy and long conversation, but they disallowed it, asking among other things that he first anathematize the Anglican Articles. Newman says he published the book for its picture of the Russian Church as Palmer met it among priests, laymen and people. It is a primary source for the early contacts between the Oxford Movement and Russian Orthodoxy, and Orthodox, Anglican and Catholic historians read it with different questions in mind.

This is No. 55 of Lérins Newman, in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. The journal is Palmer’s, and it appears under his name, edited by Newman. Newman’s own part is the selection and arrangement and the Prefatory Notice. The site’s library holds the NewmanReader transcription of that Notice from the 1882 volume, and the text is set from it. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on Palmer, his visits to Russia and his friendship with Newman, and explanatory notes on the persons, places and church terms the text names. Newman’s notes are kept as he left them.

title: Sayings of Cardinal Newman
author: John Henry Newman
lead: Short speeches and sermons from Newman’s Catholic life, from a Birmingham lecture on poetry in 1849 to his last reply to an address in July 1890, many of them as the newspapers reported them.
description: Sayings of Cardinal Newman, gathered in 1890, is a collection of speeches and sermons that John Henry Newman delivered on occasions of interest during his Catholic life. It begins with a lecture on the characteristics of poetry given at St. Chad’s Schools, Birmingham, in 1849, and ends with his reply to the Catholic Truth Society at its Birmingham conference in July 1890, headed For the last Time. Between them come remarks on receiving converts from Anglicanism, on leaving the rectorship of the Catholic University of Ireland, on writing the Apologia, at the funeral of Henry Wilberforce, and on his elevation to the Sacred College. There are words to the boys of the Oratory School, the sermons of In an Oxford Pulpit again, and his reply on Mr. Ouless’s portrait of him.

Most of the occasions are public and modest, an address from a parish, a school prize day, a visit from a society, and Newman’s answers are brief. Read together, they show the old Cardinal thanking his well-wishers and speaking of the relations between Catholics and Protestants in England, of the need of discipline, and of the conversion of England. The Oxford sermons were preached at St. Aloysius on 23 May 1880, while he was the guest of Trinity College, which had made him an Honorary Fellow two years before. They were the first he had preached in any Oxford pulpit since he left the Church of England. The book is less a work than a record, and its use is in showing how Newman spoke when he was not writing.

This is No. 56 of Lérins Newman, in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. The book holds Newman’s words at one remove. Some pieces give his replies in the first person, as he spoke or wrote them. Many others are reports of his speeches and sermons in the third person, written by those who heard them, and the short accounts of each occasion are the reporters’ and the compiler’s. The text is set from the NewmanReader transcription of the 1890 collection held in the site’s library. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the occasions and the reporting behind them, and explanatory notes on people, places and events. Any notes in the original are kept as they were left.

title: Addresses to Cardinal Newman with His Replies
author: John Henry Newman
lead: The addresses that reached Newman from colleges, chapters, societies and whole countries when Leo XIII made him a Cardinal in 1879, with his replies, among them the Biglietto Speech against liberalism in religion.
description: Addresses to Cardinal Newman with His Replies collects the congratulations sent to John Henry Newman from 1879 to 1881, after Pope Leo XIII raised him to the Sacred College, together with what he said or wrote in answer. It was prepared by Father William P. Neville of the Birmingham Oratory, long Newman’s close companion, and printed from his manuscript after Neville’s death, with an Advertisement dated 17 July 1905. Neville’s Prefatory Narrative introduces the replies. The addresses come from the Jesuits of St. Beuno’s, the Benedictines of Downside, the chapters of Birmingham and Westminster, Trinity College, Oxford, the Catholic University of Ireland, and from Ireland, Australia and the United States. The book also records the Biglietto Speech, given at the Palazzo della Pigna in Rome on 12 May 1879.

The Biglietto Speech is the chief piece, and the one most often quoted. Receiving the notice of his elevation, Newman said that for thirty, forty, fifty years he had resisted to the best of his powers “the spirit of liberalism in religion.” He defined it as the doctrine that there is no positive truth in religion, and that one creed is as good as another. The replies that follow are shorter and more personal. He speaks to schoolboys and seminarians, to the Catholic Union and the Catholic Young Men’s Societies, to the clergy of Lancashire and to the people of the Oratory mission. Together they show how Newman understood the honour, and what he chose to say about his life’s work near its end.

This is No. 57 of Lérins Newman, the last title in its part of collected essays, sketches and verse. Most of the words in the book are other people’s. The addresses are the work of the bodies that sent them, and the narrative that links them is Neville’s. Newman’s part is his replies, spoken or written, the Biglietto Speech among them. The text is set from the NewmanReader transcription of Neville’s 1905 volume held in the site’s library, with its appendix of letters. The Editors of Mere Catholicity add a new introduction on the cardinalate and the making of the book, and explanatory notes on the senders and occasions. Neville’s notes and Newman’s are kept as they were left.
